Each computer drives the same surfaces on both sides, drawn on one side only; lines to the spoilers pass over the flaps behind them, and a pitch line ends between the THS and the elevator: one computer drives both. hydraulics-users.title: Main hydraulic users

pneumatics-bleed-page.title: Bleed air on a simplified BLEED page

explanation.confuseWith: The DMCs process the data for the screens; the SDAC only gathers and concentrates it.
explanation.text: System Data Acquisition Concentrator. The aircraft has two identical SDACs. They gather data from the aircraft systems and turn it into signals for two users. The three DMCs use part of it to draw the system pages and the engine parameters on the ECAM screens, and the FWCs use the rest to produce ECAM messages and aural alerts. The SDAC itself draws nothing and decides on no warning; it only gathers and concentrates the data.

options.text: System Data Alert Concentrator
System Data Acquisition Concentrator
System Display Acquisition Computer
Signal Data Acquisition Controller

questions.stem: What does SDAC stand for?

explanation.confuseWith: The EIU is the interface between an engine's FADEC and the aircraft; the ECB belongs to the APU.
explanation.text: Electronic Control Box. The ECB is the APU's full-authority digital controller: it runs most of the APU logic, the start sequence included. For example, when the APU bleed valve is open and a cabin zone cannot reach its temperature, the air conditioning controller asks the ECB for more APU air flow. After a DC BAT BUS fault the ECB is no longer powered, so the APU cannot be started on its battery.

options.text: Engine Control Board
Electrical Control Breaker
Electronic Computing Box
Electronic Control Box

questions.stem: For the APU, what does ECB stand for?

explanation.confuseWith: The FMA is on the PFD and shows modes; the FCU on the glareshield is where the crew selects them.
explanation.text: Flight Mode Annunciator, the strip of five columns at the top of the PFD. It shows the autothrust mode, the vertical and lateral modes engaged and armed, the approach capability, and in the last column whether the AP, FD and A/THR are engaged. A mode change shows there first, so reading it aloud is how the crew confirms what the automation is really doing.

options.text: Flight Management Annunciator
Flight Mode Alert
Flight Monitoring Area
Flight Mode Annunciator

questions.stem: What does FMA stand for?

explanation.confuseWith: The PTU never moves fluid between green and yellow; the danger is heat, not fluid transfer.
explanation.text: Switching the PTU off protects the healthy system. With a low reservoir level, the PTU may overheat about two minutes later, and the heat can then take out the yellow system too, turning one failure into a dual hydraulic failure. The same applies to a reservoir overheat, and to low reservoir air pressure when the pressure fluctuates. Fluid never passes from one system to another; the PTU only lets one system's pressure drive a pump on the other.

options.text: Yellow fluid would flow into the green reservoir
The RAT would extend automatically
A PTU overheat that may also cost the yellow system
The blue system would lose pressure through the PTU

questions.stem: After HYD G RSVR LO LVL, the ECAM asks for the PTU to be switched off without delay. What could happen if it kept running?

explanation.confuseWith: Thrust levers at TOGA alone is the normal go-around; the G+Y STATUS adds the reduction to MCT.
explanation.text: Maximum pitch 15°, with the thrust levers at TOGA and then MCT. The stabiliser is lost in this failure, so pitch is controlled by the elevators alone, and after the gravity gear extension the aircraft is in direct law without auto trim. The same STATUS page also asks the crew to manoeuvre with care and limits the speed to 320 kt or M 0.77. The thrust line is not shown when one engine is inoperative.

options.text: Max pitch 20°; thrust levers TOGA then CL
Max pitch 10°; thrust levers MCT only
Max pitch 15°; thrust levers TOGA then MCT
Max pitch 15°; thrust levers TOGA only

questions.stem: HYD G+Y SYS LO PR, both engines running. What does the STATUS page give for a go-around?

explanation.confuseWith: The 400 ft guideline is for READ & DO actions; memory items are not delayed.
explanation.text: For take-off and go-around, the FCTM delays READ & DO actions until at least 400 ft AGL, which balances time to stabilise the aircraft against waiting too long. A safe flight path is the first priority, so the crew may start below 400 ft once the flight path is safe. Memory items are different: they are applied at once from memory in time-critical situations.

options.text: At once after lift-off, whatever the flight path
Normally from 400 ft AGL, or earlier if the flight path is safe
Only once above 1 000 ft AGL
Only after the thrust reduction altitude

questions.stem: A failure occurs shortly after lift-off. When should the crew start the READ & DO actions of the ECAM?

explanation.confuseWith: The RAT keeps the blue system alive, but blue powers the slats and some flight controls, not the brakes.
explanation.text: Green and yellow are not pressurised without engines, and the RAT feeds only blue, which has no brakes. What is left is the brake accumulator on the yellow side. Anti-skid and nosewheel steering are inoperative, so brake pressure is limited to 1 000 PSI to reduce the risk of a locked wheel and a burst tyre, and the stored energy gives at least seven full applications. Reversers are not available either, so the stop depends on careful pedal braking.

options.text: Yellow accumulator with anti-skid, with no limit on applications
Yellow accumulator only: 7 full applications, 1 000 PSI max
Alternate braking on the blue system, with anti-skid
Normal braking, powered by the RAT through the green system

questions.stem: ALL ENG FAIL, forced landing on a runway. What braking is available after touchdown?

explanation.confuseWith: At this step one ADR stays on and two are switched off, so the flight laws cannot use two wrong ADRs that agree.
explanation.text: When no ADR can be trusted, the barometric altitude may be wrong as well, and the transponder would keep sending it to ATC and to the TCAS of other aircraft. The procedure therefore switches altitude reporting off once the ADR selection is done, and the crew tells ATC about the situation without delay. The flight then continues on the pitch/thrust tables, or on the backup speed scale where the aircraft has one.

options.text: True
False

questions.stem: UNRELIABLE SPEED INDICATION: the affected ADRs cannot be identified. The procedure asks the crew to set ATC/XPDR ALT RPTG to OFF. True or false?

explanation.confuseWith: Clearing the ECAM procedure early is what lets a lower-priority alert take the crew's attention.
explanation.text: When the ECAM sends the crew to the QRH, the ECAM procedure stays on the display while the QRH procedure is applied. If it were cleared, the next alert in the queue, of lower priority, would appear and could pull the crew's attention away from the procedure in progress. Once the QRH procedure is done, the crew returns to the ECAM and goes on as usual.

options.text: Keep it, but read the STATUS page first
Clear it, and recall it after the QRH procedure
Clear it, so that the next alert can be read
Keep it displayed while the QRH procedure is applied

questions.stem: An ECAM procedure asks the crew to apply a QRH procedure. What should be done with the ECAM procedure meanwhile?

explanation.confuseWith: 2.5 % is the shift for ten passengers moved from the middle of the cabin, not from the front.
explanation.text: An aft CG helps keep the nose off the runway after touchdown, so the crew can lower it gently before elevator control is lost. The QRH gives the effect of moving passengers: ten passengers from the front to the rear move the CG roughly 4 % aft, and ten from the middle to the rear about 2.5 %. After touchdown the nose is held up with the elevator and the brakes are applied smoothly.

options.text: About 1 %
About 8 %
About 4 %
About 2.5 %

questions.stem: LANDING WITH ABNORMAL L/G with the nose gear abnormal. The procedure asks to shift the CG aft. About how far aft does moving 10 passengers from the front to the rear move it?

explanation.confuseWith: Leaving the pedals alone is right only when A/BRK MAX is actually decelerating the aircraft, above 72 kt.
explanation.text: Below 72 kt the ground spoilers do not deploy, and the autobrake, which is triggered by their extension, does not act. So the captain reduces the thrust and at the same moment applies maximum pressure on both pedals, keeping them fully pressed until the aircraft stops. Above 72 kt with A/BRK MAX working, the opposite applies: the captain avoids pressing the pedals by reflex.

options.text: Gradual pedal braking to avoid a tyre burst
No pedal braking: autobrake MAX stops the aircraft
Reverse only, then pedal braking below 30 kt
Full pedal pressure on both brakes while reducing thrust, held to the stop

questions.stem: The take-off is rejected at 60 kt with autobrake MAX armed. How does the captain brake?

explanation.confuseWith: Setting TA ONLY is a measure for an engine failure, not for an emergency descent, where TA/RA stays selected.
explanation.text: Yes. The FCTM keeps the TCAS in TA/RA during an emergency descent, because that mode gives the most protection against collision, and avoiding a collision comes first even if the descent must stop for a while. After the RA the descent is resumed. Below FL 100 the crew then limits the rate of descent to about 1 000 ft/min, except in the approach phase.

options.text: No: the emergency descent has priority over the RA
Yes: collision avoidance has priority over the descent

questions.stem: During an EMER DESCENT the TCAS gives an RA that interrupts the descent. Should the crew follow it?

explanation.confuseWith: One pack OFF is the first step; above 9 PSI both packs go OFF and the crew lands as soon as possible.
explanation.text: With a total loss of pressure control causing overpressure, the crew first sets one pack OFF and both ventilation BLOWER and EXTRACT to OVRD, so that cabin air goes overboard, and watches ΔP. If ΔP still exceeds 9 PSI, both packs go OFF and the aircraft lands as soon as possible. 10 min before landing both packs are OFF, and before a door is opened ΔP is checked at zero.

options.text: Keep one pack OFF and continue the flight
Land as soon as possible, with both packs OFF
Set MAN mode and open the outflow valve
Descend to FL 100 and continue

questions.stem: [QRH] CABIN OVERPRESSURE: one pack is already OFF with the ventilation at OVRD, and ΔP is still above 9 PSI. What does the procedure ask?

explanation.confuseWith: CONF FULL is avoided because it would make the jammed-stabiliser aircraft harder to handle.
explanation.text: Without manual trim, CONF FULL is not selected, because it would degrade the handling qualities; the landing is made with the flap lever at 3, with GPWS LDG FLAP 3 set ON to avoid a nuisance TOO LOW FLAPS alert. The approach capability is CAT 1 only. If manual trim is available, the crew instead trims to keep the elevator at its neutral position on the F/CTL SD page.

options.text: FLAP lever 3, GPWS LDG FLAP 3 ON, CAT 1 only
CONF FULL with GPWS FLAP MODE OFF
FLAP lever 3, CAT 2 allowed
CONF FULL, CAT 3 SINGLE allowed

questions.stem: [QRH] STABILIZER JAM, manual pitch trim not available. Which landing configuration and approach?

explanation.confuseWith: 200 kt is the limit with a cockpit window open; 250 kt would exceed it.
explanation.text: If visibility is not enough for the approach, the crew first considers an autoland. Without it, the cabin pressure mode goes to MAN with the V/S control full up, the speed is kept at or below 200 kt and the PF opens the sliding window to look out. 200 kt is the cockpit window open limit. With the higher noise, the crew watches visual warnings closely.

options.text: Set the windshield heating to maximum to clear it
Keep 250 kt or less and open the PF window
Depressurise, keep 200 kt or less, open the PF window
Run the wipers at maximum speed throughout

questions.stem: Damaged windshield and no autoland available. How does the PF get a view for the approach?

explanation.confuseWith: The fast rate is for leaving the high altitude; below FL 100 the descent is slowed.
explanation.text: Below FL 100 the FCTM recommends a gentler descent of about 1 000 ft/min, the approach phase being the exception. During the whole descent the TCAS stays at TA/RA, since avoiding a collision comes first. Once the oxygen masks are taken off, the crew closes the mask stowage and presses the PRESS TO RESET slide to stop the oxygen and the mask microphone.

options.text: The same rate, down to MEA-MORA
About 1 000 ft/min, except in the approach phase
About 500 ft/min in every phase
About 3 000 ft/min, to save time

questions.stem: After an emergency descent, the aircraft passes FL 100. What rate of descent does the FCTM suggest from there?

explanation.confuseWith: One reset at a time is the rule for authorised resets, not a way round a forbidden one.
explanation.text: No reset is authorised. When several failures concern the same system, one forbidden reset is enough to forbid them all. When a reset is allowed, the crew applies one at a time, with the specific procedure of the table or the standard reset procedure, and never from memory. On the ground, by contrast, a system that the table does not list may also be reset.

options.text: Both may be reset, but only one at a time
The authorised reset may be done for the first failure
No reset of that system is authorised
The authorised reset may be done, but only on the ground

questions.stem: Two failures affect the same system. The reset table authorises a reset for one of them, but not for the other. What applies?

explanation.confuseWith: Red LAND ASAP still needs an airport where the landing is safe, not just any airport.
explanation.text: Red LAND ASAP asks for a landing as soon as possible at the closest airport that allows a safe landing. For ELEC EMER CONFIG the FCTM adds that flying an approach to a badly equipped field with marginal weather would not be wise, while a long flight in this configuration is not recommended either. The flight is hand-flown, in alternate law and then direct law with the gear down, and the workload is high.

options.text: Land there, as red LAND ASAP ignores the weather
Avoid that airport, but do not prolong the flight either
Hold until the batteries recharge, then decide
Continue to destination, as the RAT can run for hours

questions.stem: ELEC EMER CONFIG in cruise. The ECAM shows LAND ASAP in red. The nearest airport is poorly equipped and its weather is marginal. What does the FCTM say?

explanation.confuseWith: A normal go-around from CONF 3 retracts one step to CONF 2; the overweight procedure asks for CONF 1+F.
explanation.text: CONF 1+F. When an overweight landing is made in a configuration other than FULL, the procedure asks for CONF 1+F in a go-around. For the approach, packs 1 and 2 are set OFF or supplied by the APU, which raises the maximum thrust the engines can give if a go-around is needed. FULL is the normal landing setting, unless a procedure or the landing performance limits it.

options.text: CONF 3
CONF 2
CONF 1
CONF 1+F

questions.stem: [QRH] OVERWEIGHT LANDING: the landing is planned in CONF 3. Which configuration is used for a go-around?

explanation.confuseWith: Where cargo ventilation is fitted, an extraction fan draws cabin air through the cargo holds; they are not conditioned zones.
explanation.text: Cockpit, forward cabin and aft cabin: the air conditioning system feeds these three zones and controls each one independently. Air from the pneumatic system passes the two pack flow control valves and the two packs, then reaches the mixing unit, where it joins recirculated cabin air. From there it is distributed to the cockpit and the cabin. Each zone has a temperature of its own, selected on the AIR COND panel.

options.text: Cockpit, cargo bays and cabin
Cockpit, fwd and aft cabins
Cockpit, avionics bay and cabin
Cockpit, cabin and holds 1 and 2 only

questions.stem: Conditioned air is distributed to:

explanation.confuseWith: 24 °C is the backup regulation after a primary channel failure only, not the result of a double failure.
explanation.text: 20 °C from pack 1 and 10 °C from pack 2: with both channels of the zone controller failed, optimised and backup regulation are both lost, so each pack falls back to a fixed outlet temperature. The ECAM COND page then loses all its information and shows PACK REG. This differs from a primary channel failure alone, where the secondary channel keeps the zones at 24 °C, pack 1 for the cockpit and pack 2 for the cabin.

options.text: 15 °C both
25 °C both
20 °C for pack one and 10 °C for pack two
24 °C for pack one and 15 °C for pack two

questions.stem: In case of zone controller primary and secondary channel failure, what temperatures are maintained by pack one and pack two?

explanation.confuseWith: The similar rule for bleed air bans the APU bleed together with a high-pressure air start unit.
explanation.text: No: the crew must never run the packs while a low-pressure air conditioning unit is also supplying air. The limitation exists to protect the air conditioning system. Both sources feed the same mixing unit, which has low-pressure ground inlets of its own. The rule has no exception for hot airfields, outside temperature or ground cart flow.

options.text: Yes
No
Yes, if external temperature is greater than 50 °C
Yes, provided the airflow supplied by the ground cart is less than 1.2 kg/s

questions.stem: It is permissible to use simultaneously packs and LP ground unit during long stops in a hot airfield

explanation.confuseWith: A low passenger load calls for LO, not HI; more flow is never selected to warm the cabin.
explanation.text: HI is for hot conditions with many people on board: it gives 120 % of normal pack flow, which helps cool the cabin. The selector sets the flow for the number of occupants and the outside conditions. The cockpit preparation procedure uses HI for abnormally hot and humid conditions, LO with fewer than 141 occupants and NORM otherwise. HI is also used for smoke removal.

options.text: In cold conditions to achieve a higher cabin temperature range.
With a low passenger load to increase cabin air flow.
With a high passenger load in hot conditions in order to help reduce the cabin temperature.
With a low passenger load to reduce bleed air demand.

questions.stem: Under what conditions should the pack flow controller be set to HI?

explanation.confuseWith: Cold weather never raises the flow; the only automatic increase from LO is to 100 %, when cooling demand is not met.
explanation.text: Because the APU is the only bleed source: whenever the APU supplies the bleed air, HI flow is selected automatically, whatever the PACK FLOW selector shows. The same applies in single-pack operation. The crew's LO, NORM or HI choice only counts with both packs running on engine bleed air. Even then, a LO selection is raised to normal flow automatically if the temperature demand cannot be met.

options.text: As the engines are not running the PACK FLOW indicators are at the position they were selected to at the last shut down.
As no bleed air is flowing the PACK FLOW valves are spring loaded to the fully open position.
HI flow is automatically selected regardless of PACK FLOW selector position because air is only being supplied by the APU.
With cold outside air conditions the PACK FLOW is automatically increased to help increase the cabin temperature.

questions.stem: The PACK FLOW controller is set to NORM and yet the ECAM display shows PACK FLOW to be high. How is this possible?

explanation.confuseWith: The FAULT light in the APU MASTER SW pushbutton is the one that reports a failed APU or an automatic shutdown.
explanation.text: False: the APU BLEED FAULT light does not report a failed APU controller. It comes on, with an ECAM caution, when the system detects a leak in the APU bleed duct. With the X BLEED selector at AUTO, such a leak also closes the crossbleed valve. A failed APU, or an automatic shutdown, is shown instead by the FAULT light of the APU MASTER SW pushbutton.

options.text: True.
False.

questions.stem: The APU BLEED FAULT indicates that the main APU controller is in fault.

explanation.confuseWith: Only one of the three motors drives the valve at a time; they are independent, not linked.
explanation.text: One of three electric motors: the outflow valve actuator holds three independent motors, two for automatic operation and one for manual operation, and any one of them can drive the valve. Normally the active cabin pressure controller works the valve through its own automatic motor. When the crew selects MAN, power to the automatic motors is cut and the manual motor takes over.

options.text: One of two electric motors.
One of three electric motors.
Three mechanically linked electric motors.
Two of three electric motors working together.

questions.stem: The outflow valve is powered by:

explanation.confuseWith: The engine bleed valves are not on the ditching list; the packs are shut at their flow control valves.
explanation.text: All of them: with DITCHING ON, the operating pressure controller orders the outflow valve, the pack flow control valves, the emergency ram air inlet and both avionics ventilation valves (inlet and extract) to close; on some aircraft the forward cargo outlet valve too. Closing every opening below the waterline keeps the fuselage watertight. Under manual pressure control, the outflow valve does not close automatically.

options.text: Outflow valve
Ram air inlet and ventilation extract valves
The pack flow control valves
All of the above

questions.stem: The ditching switch when selected sends a closure signal to:

explanation.confuseWith: 8 800 ft only makes the cabin altitude pulse green; red comes above 9 550 ft.
explanation.text: Above 9 550 ft: the cabin altitude figure on the CAB PRESS page turns red once the cabin is higher than 9 550 ft, which is also the excess cabin altitude warning in cruise. Before that, from 8 800 ft, the figure pulses as an advisory. Normally the system keeps the cabin at about 8 000 ft at most in cruise.

questions.stem: On ECAM Cab. press page, the cabin altitude indication changes to red when cabin altitude is:

explanation.confuseWith: RAM AIR is not part of this procedure; once manual control has failed to open the valve, the step is both packs OFF.
explanation.text: The alert comes on the ground when the outflow valve has not fully opened within its 70 s delay. The crew first drives the valve open in manual mode, allowing about 5 s to see it move. If that fails, both packs are switched off. Before the cabin crew opens a door, the flight crew must confirm that no residual pressure difference is left.

options.text: DITCHING ON
PACK 1 and PACK 2 OFF
Open a passenger door slowly
RAM AIR ON

questions.stem: CAB PR OFV NOT OPEN on the ground. MODE SEL MAN and MAN V/S CTL FULL UP have not opened the outflow valve. What next?

explanation.confuseWith: The outflow valve opens to about 50 % only below 1 PSI and in automatic mode; at 3 PSI its control stays normal.
explanation.text: No air flows yet. The door of the emergency ram air inlet opens when the pb is pressed, but a check valve behind it stays closed while the cabin pressure is more than 1 PSI above the outside pressure. Below 1 PSI, with the pressure in automatic mode, the outflow valve opens to about half, and outside air then flows into the mixer unit.

options.text: Ram air, mixed with pack air in the mixer unit
Ram air, but only to the avionics bay
None, as the check valve stays shut above 1 PSI
Full ram air, as the inlet door is open

questions.stem: Smoke removal in flight: RAM AIR is ON and the cabin differential pressure is still 3 PSI. What air comes in through the ram air inlet?

explanation.confuseWith: 750 ft/min is the maximum cabin descent rate in the descent mode, not the release rate at touchdown.
explanation.text: The controller lets the remaining pressure out gradually, with the cabin climbing at 500 ft/min. Only 55 s after landing does the ground function open the outflow valve fully, which makes sure no pressure is left before the doors are opened. In manual mode none of this happens: the outflow valve does not open by itself at touchdown, so the crew controls it.

options.text: Gradually, at the maximum cabin rate of 750 ft/min
Gradually, at a cabin vertical speed of 500 ft/min
By the outflow valve opening fully at touchdown
By the safety valves, which open at touchdown

questions.stem: In automatic mode, how is the cabin pressure that remains at touchdown released?

explanation.confuseWith: One pb at OVRD gives closed circuit with added air conditioning air; only both at OVRD send the air overboard.
explanation.text: With both pbs at OVRD, the avionics are cooled by air conditioning air that passes once through the bay and is then thrown overboard. The blower fan stops and the extract fan keeps running, and the air leaves the aircraft instead of going round the closed circuit. With only one pb at OVRD, the system stays in closed circuit and adds air conditioning air instead.

options.text: From the air conditioning system, then overboard
From outside through the skin inlet, then overboard
From the air conditioning system, then under the cargo floor
Round the closed circuit, through the skin heat exchanger

questions.stem: Avionics smoke: the BLOWER and EXTRACT pbs are both set to OVRD. Where does the cooling air come from, and where does it go?

explanation.confuseWith: The Warsaw Convention deals with an airline's liability to passengers and cargo, not with founding ICAO.
explanation.text: The Chicago Convention, the Convention on International Civil Aviation signed in 1944. It set up ICAO, which works through standards and recommended practices published in the annexes to the convention. The other conventions deal with narrower subjects: Warsaw and Montreal 1999 with the liability of carriers, Tokyo with offences on board. The states that signed it agreed to follow the annexes or to notify ICAO of any difference.

options.text: The Warsaw Convention of 1929
The Tokyo Convention of 1963
The Montreal Convention of 1999
The Chicago Convention of 1944

questions.stem: Which international convention created ICAO?

explanation.confuseWith: 39 000 ft is a start limit with the normal electrical supply on one APU type, not the limit for a start on batteries.
explanation.text: With the batteries as the only power source, the APU may be started in flight up to 25 000 ft. The figure is the same for both APU types. With the normal electrical supply the start limit is much higher: 39 000 ft or 41 000 ft, depending on the APU type. Within those limits, APU starts are allowed throughout the normal flight envelope.

questions.stem: What is the maximum altitude at which the APU may be started using the batteries only?

explanation.confuseWith: The APU fuel pump has no tank of its own: it only boosts the pressure in the left fuel feed line when the tank pumps cannot.
explanation.text: The APU takes its fuel from the left fuel feed line. The tank pumps normally keep that line under pressure. When they cannot, on batteries only or with the pumps off, the APU fuel pump starts by itself and supplies the start. The ECB then meters the flow. The MASTER SW opens the APU fuel isolation valve, and the APU FIRE pushbutton closes the low-pressure fuel valve.

options.text: Left fuel feed line.
Right fuel feed line.
Left or right fuel line
Center tank, through a separate APU feed line.

questions.stem: The APU is supplied from the:

explanation.confuseWith: In flight a start on batteries only is limited to 25 000 ft.
explanation.text: Yes, the APU can be started on the ground with the aircraft batteries as the only source. While the MASTER SW is ON and APU speed is below 95 %, the battery charge limiters connect the batteries to the DC BAT bus for the start. The start should be made within about 30 minutes of setting the batteries to AUTO, since after 35 minutes their charge falls below a quarter.

options.text: Yes
No

questions.stem: On ground, can you start the APU using the aircraft batteries only?

explanation.confuseWith: Ignition comes 1.5 s after the starter is energised; it is not a condition before it.
explanation.text: The ECB energises the starter only once the air intake flap is completely open, with MASTER SW and START both ON. Opening the flap is one of the first steps after MASTER SW is pressed, together with the ECB power-up test and the fuel isolation valve. The ignition follows 1.5 s after the starter, not before it. The APU fuel pump runs only when no tank pump is running.

options.text: The air intake flap must be fully open
The APU speed must have reached 7 %
The ignition must have been on for 1.5 s
The APU fuel pump must be running

questions.stem: During an APU start, what must happen before the starter is energised?

explanation.confuseWith: Information such as traffic or wind is acknowledged, not read back word for word; codes, levels and frequencies are.
explanation.text: SSR codes are always read back, because an error in them is dangerous. The same applies to altimeter settings and transition levels; level, heading and speed instructions; new frequencies; route clearances; the runway in use; and any clearance to enter, cross, take off from, land on, taxi or backtrack on, or hold short of a runway. A wrong code would show the controller false identity or emergency data, and the read-back lets the error be caught at once.

options.text: A runway braking action report
Traffic information about other aircraft
The surface wind passed with a landing clearance
An SSR code

questions.stem: Under SERA, which of these items must the flight crew always read back?

explanation.confuseWith: Class C is the class where IFR flights are also separated from VFR flights.
explanation.text: In Class D both IFR and VFR flights need a clearance and continuous radio, but ATC separates IFR flights only from other IFR flights. For VFR traffic, the IFR crew receives traffic information, and avoidance advice on request. So in Class D the crew of an airliner keeps a visual lookout for VFR traffic, especially below 10 000 ft, where a 250 kt limit applies to all flights.

options.text: VFR flights only
IFR and VFR flights
Other IFR flights only
No flights: it receives traffic information only

questions.stem: In Class D airspace, from which flights is an IFR flight separated by ATC?

explanation.confuseWith: The SID designator gives the lateral route; the climb comes only with a cleared level.
explanation.text: No. Under ICAO, a SID or STAR designator on its own does not authorise a climb or descent along the procedure's vertical profile. The crew needs a cleared level. Once a level is given, the SID's published restrictions apply on the way up to it. If the clearance contains no level, the crew asks ATC for one.

options.text: Yes
No

questions.stem: Under ICAO rules, the departure clearance gives a SID designator but no cleared level. Does it allow the crew to climb along the SID's vertical profile?

explanation.confuseWith: "You may proceed" is shown by an abrupt climbing breakaway turn, not by rocking the wings.
explanation.text: Rocking the wings and flashing navigation lights from slightly above and ahead, normally on the left, means "You have been intercepted. Follow me." The intercepted aircraft answers in the same way, rocking and flashing its lights, and follows. The crew also calls on 121.5 MHz and, if possible, tells ATS. An abrupt climbing breakaway turn of 90° or more means "You may proceed".

options.text: You may proceed
Land at this aerodrome
You are entering a prohibited area; turn back
You have been intercepted; follow me

questions.stem: An intercepting military aircraft, slightly ahead and above on the left, rocks its wings and then makes a slow level turn. What does it mean?

explanation.confuseWith: NEGATIVE means no, not permitted or not correct; it does not mean "I cannot comply".
explanation.text: UNABLE tells ATC the crew cannot do what was asked, instructed or cleared, and is normally followed by the reason, for example performance or weather. Controllers use it too when traffic does not allow a requested change, and may offer an alternative route or level.

options.text: WILCO, followed by an alternative
NEGATIVE, followed by the instruction repeated
UNABLE, normally followed by a reason
STANDBY, followed by the crew's intentions

questions.stem: A crew cannot comply with an ATC instruction. Which standard word is used, and what normally follows it?

explanation.confuseWith: Class C is where an IFR flight is separated from VFR flights too.
explanation.text: Traffic information on VFR flights, and traffic avoidance advice when requested. In Class D only IFR flights are separated from each other; VFR flights are not separated from anyone. VFR flights, in turn, receive traffic information on all other flights. Every flight needs an ATC clearance and keeps to 250 kt IAS below 10 000 ft AMSL.

options.text: No information about VFR traffic
Traffic information, and avoidance advice on request
Separation from every VFR flight
Separation from VFR flights at night only

questions.stem: Under SERA, in Class D airspace, what does an IFR flight receive about VFR traffic?

explanation.confuseWith: AP, FD and A/THR commands belong to the flight guidance part of the FMGC, not to the flight management part.
explanation.text: The FM part looks after navigation, flight planning, and performance optimisation with its predictions. It also manages the navigation radios and the displays. The other part of each FMGC, the FG part, commands the AP, the FDs and the A/THR. Each FMGC carries its own databases, among them the navigation and performance databases.

options.text: Navigation, flight planning and A/THR commands.
Performance optimization, A/THR and AP commands
Navigation, flight planning, performance optimization and flight predictions
AP and FD commands and flight envelope computation.

questions.stem: The Flight Management part of the FMGC includes the following elements:

explanation.confuseWith: A dash marks an FD switched off by the crew; the same number on both sides marks a failed FD with the other one serving both PFDs.
explanation.text: The FMA tells a switched-off FD from a failed one. -FD2 means the crew has switched FD1 off: its pushbutton goes off, its bars leave PFD 1, and FD2 stays engaged. 2FD2 means FD1 has failed: the FD pushbuttons stay on and both PFDs show the guidance of the remaining FD2. The same logic applies the other way round, with 1FD- and 1FD1.

options.text: FD1 failed, FD2 engaged. FD1 switched off, FD2 used by both PFDs.
FD1 switched off, FD2 engaged. FD1 failed, FD2 used by both PFDs.
FD2 switched off, FD1 engaged. FD2 failed, FD1 used by both PFDs.
FD2 failed, FD1 engaged. FD2 switched off, FD1 used by both PFDs.

questions.stem: What is the difference between -FD2 and 2FD2 on the FMA?

explanation.confuseWith: On the other display standard, DMC 1 drives both ECAM displays and DMC 2 only the First Officer's PFD and ND.
explanation.text: On this display standard each side has its own DMC, and the two ECAM screens are split between them. DMC 1 drives the Captain's PFD and ND and the upper ECAM display; DMC 2 drives the First Officer's PFD and ND and the lower ECAM display. DMC 3 stands by: with the EIS DMC selector on the switching panel at CAPT 3 or F/O 3, it replaces a failed DMC 1 or 2.

options.text: DMC #1 supplies data to PFD #2, ND #2 and LOWER ECAM. DMC #2 supplies data for PFD #1, ND #1, and UPPER ECAM.
ADMC #1 supplies data to PFD #1, ND #1 and LOWER ECAM. DMC #2 supplies data for PFD #2, ND #2, and UPPER ECAM.
DMC #1 supplies data to PFD #1, ND #1, and UPPER ECAM. DMC #2 supplies data for PFD #2, ND #2, and LOWER ECAM.
DMC #1 supplies data to PFD #1, ND #1 and LOWER ECAM. DMC #2 supplies data for PFD #2, ND #2, and LOWER ECAM.

questions.stem: Where is the information displayed by DMC #1 and DMC #2 (aircraft where each DMC drives one ECAM display)?

explanation.confuseWith: The ECAM/ND XFR selector moves the system display onto an ND; it does not replace a failed DMC.
explanation.text: Turning the EIS DMC selector on the switching panel puts DMC 3, the standby unit, in place of the failed one: CAPT 3 replaces DMC 1 and F/O 3 replaces DMC 2. Without it, the PFD and ND of the failed DMC stay lost. The display unit failure procedure asks the crew to consider this DMC switching when a diagonal line appears on a display.

options.text: Once a DMC has failed the information is unrecoverable
No action is needed as recovery is automatic.
Rotate the EIS DMC switch on the switching panel to replace the failed DMC with DMC #3.
Use the ECAM/ND XFR switch to move the failed displays to the other DMC.

questions.stem: After a single DMC failure, how could a crewmember recover the display units?

explanation.confuseWith: LOC and G/S arm when APPR is pressed; capture comes later, when the beams are reached.
explanation.text: Pressing APPR arms LOC and G/S only above 400 ft RA, and only when the aircraft is not in the take-off or go-around SRS mode. One LS receiver is enough; with two, both must carry the same LS data. LOC also needs HDG/TRK or NAV engaged. The 2 dot figure belongs to the glide slope capture zone, which comes after arming.

options.text: Above 400 ft RA, and both LS receivers are operative
Within 2 dots of the localiser, and NAV is engaged
Above 400 ft RA, and the vertical mode is not SRS
Above 1 000 ft RA, and the vertical mode is not SRS

questions.stem: ILS approach set on the ARRIVAL page. When the crew presses APPR, which condition must also be met for LOC and G/S to arm?

explanation.confuseWith: The PROG figure assumes long-range cruise speed; the drift-down ceiling assumes green dot, the obstacle strategy speed.
explanation.text: With an engine out, the FMS works out the highest level it can hold at long-range cruise speed and shows it on PROG; it suits the standard strategy, flown faster. The engine-out PERF CRZ page shows the drift-down ceiling, the highest level that can be held at green dot, which is the speed of the obstacle strategy. The drift-down ceiling is the one that matters when terrain is the concern.

options.text: PROG: the drift-down ceiling at green dot; PERF CRZ: at long-range cruise speed
Both are at green dot; PROG adds a 300 ft/min margin
PROG: at long-range cruise speed; PERF CRZ: the drift-down ceiling at green dot
Both are the same figure, shown on two pages

questions.stem: Engine failure in cruise. What is the difference between the engine-out maximum altitude on the PROG page and the ceiling on the PERF CRZ page?

explanation.confuseWith: Below 700 ft RA an RMP cannot retune the locked ILS either.
explanation.text: Once the aircraft passes 700 ft RA with the approach modes armed or engaged and an AP or FD on, the receiver keeps the ILS frequency and course it already has. A new entry, typed on the MCDU or set on an RMP, then changes nothing in the receiver. The same lock stops PERF APPR changes from reaching the managed speed guidance.

options.text: Only a change made on the RMP is accepted
Nothing: frequency and course are frozen in the receiver
The receiver takes the new course, and LOC is lost
The course changes, and the AP disconnects

questions.stem: ILS approach with APPR engaged and an AP engaged, below 700 ft RA. The PM changes the ILS course on the MCDU. What happens?

explanation.confuseWith: THR LVR with a limited thrust is the case of levers below CL, not above it.
explanation.text: Above the CL detent with both engines, or above FLX-MCT with one engine out, the A/THR goes from active to armed. The engines then follow the levers directly, so thrust increases straight away to match their position, and the FMA shows MAN THR. Bringing the levers back into the active range, at or below CL, makes the A/THR active again.

options.text: The thrust is limited and THR LVR shows
The A/THR disconnects with an AUTO FLT A/THR OFF alert
The A/THR becomes armed, and thrust rises at once to the lever position
The A/THR stays active and keeps CLB thrust

questions.stem: Both engines running, A/THR active in CLB. The crew pushes both thrust levers above the CL detent. What happens?

explanation.confuseWith: ENABLE ALTN applies when the alternate is in the active flight plan; the SEC F-PLN prompt needs HDG.
explanation.text: Once the path is safe and the clearance obtained, the crew moves the FMS from the go-around phase toward the diversion. If the alternate route is in the secondary flight plan, it is activated and a DIR TO made as needed, but the ACTIVATE SEC F-PLN prompt is shown only with the AP/FD in HDG. If the alternate was prepared in the active flight plan, the crew uses ENABLE ALTN from a lateral revision at the TO waypoint instead.

options.text: Any mode; the prompt is always shown
GA TRK
HDG
NAV

questions.stem: After a go-around the crew diverts. The alternate route is stored in the secondary flight plan. What must the AP/FD lateral mode be for the ACTIVATE SEC F-PLN prompt to appear?

explanation.confuseWith: Pressing LOC with G/S armed drops only the glide slope and LOC stays armed; a LOC pb press disarms LOC only when G/S is not armed.
explanation.text: G/S stays armed only while the approach logic stays as it is. Pressing the LOC pb, or the APPR pb again, disarms it, and so does a lost or disarmed localiser mode, a change of approach selection, a go-around or an AP/FD TCAS engagement. G/S is also disarmed normally when G/S* engages at capture. Speed or altitude selections and the second AP have no such effect.

options.text: Engaging the second AP
Selecting a new speed on the FCU
Selecting a lower altitude on the FCU
Pressing the LOC pb

questions.stem: LOC and G/S are armed. Which of these crew actions disarms the G/S mode?

explanation.confuseWith: 2 268 is 5 000 divided by 2.2046, the conversion done in the wrong direction.
explanation.text: 11 023 lb. One kilogram is about 2.2046 lb, so the number of pounds is always larger than the number of kilograms: 5 000 × 2.2046 = 11 023. A quick mental check is to double the kilograms and add 10 %: 10 000 + 1 000 = 11 000. Dividing by 2.2 instead gives 2 268, the wrong way round (that is the kilograms in 5 000 lb).

questions.stem: About how many pounds is 5 000 kg?

explanation.confuseWith: Subtracting is the wrong way: cold air makes the aircraft lower than indicated, so the corrected altitude must be higher.
explanation.text: Add about 160 ft. In cold air the true altitude is lower than the altimeter shows, so minimum altitudes are raised. For a sea-level aerodrome the FCTM gives about 4 × Delta ISA × height ÷ 1 000: 4 × 20 × 2 = 160 ft. The correction grows with the cold and with the height above the aerodrome, and it is applied to the FAF, step-down and missed approach altitudes and the minima.

options.text: Add about 160 ft
Subtract about 160 ft
Add about 80 ft
Add about 400 ft

questions.stem: Sea-level aerodrome, Delta ISA −20 °C. By the FCTM rule of thumb, what correction applies to a minimum altitude 2 000 ft above the aerodrome?

explanation.confuseWith: About 4 min is the value for a full hour at the lower speed, not for 30 minutes.
explanation.text: About 2 minutes. The FCTM rule is that flying M 0.05 slower for one hour is worth about 4 minutes of holding. The time gained grows in proportion to how long the aircraft flies slower, so half an hour gives about 2 minutes. So a holding delay is best absorbed early, at cruise level, with ATC's agreement, not in a stack.

options.text: About 2 min
About 8 min
About 4 min
About 1 min

questions.stem: By the FCTM rule of thumb, slowing down by M 0.05 for 30 minutes absorbs about how much holding time?

explanation.confuseWith: 3 280 is the feet in 1 000 m; it is the factor for metres to feet, not a height in metres.
explanation.text: About 3 048 m. One foot is exactly 0.3048 m, so 10 000 ft × 0.3048 = 3 048 m. For a quick estimate, metres are a little under a third of the feet. 3 280 is the number of feet in 1 000 m, used for the other direction, and dividing by 3 gives a rough 3 333 m that is about 285 m too high.

questions.stem: A controller using metres asks you to climb to the equivalent of 10 000 ft. About how many metres is that?

explanation.confuseWith: 900 ft is the height for about 3 NM; each nautical mile adds roughly 300 ft.
explanation.text: About 1 300 ft. A 3° path rises about 318 ft for every nautical mile from the threshold, close to 300 ft. At 4 NM that is 4 × 318 ≈ 1 270 ft, so about 1 300 ft. Crews use this to cross-check the approach against the DME or the FMS distance. 900 ft would be the height at about 3 NM.

options.text: About 400 ft
About 1 300 ft
About 2 000 ft
About 900 ft

questions.stem: The FMS shows 4 NM to the threshold. Roughly what height above the threshold puts the aircraft on a 3° path?

explanation.confuseWith: The CIDS runs cabin functions such as lighted signs and cabin lighting; the audio management system is the crew's audio interface.
explanation.text: All of the above: the audio management system is how the crew reaches every audio service. Through it the crew transmits and listens on the installed radio communication and navigation equipment, talks on the interphones, uses the call systems and makes passenger announcements. It is built around an AMU with three ACPs, the boomsets, hand microphones, oxygen mask microphones and two cockpit loudspeakers.

options.text: All the radio communication and radio navigation facilities installed on the aircraft in transmission and reception mode.
The interphone system.
The call systems and Passenger Address (PA) system.
All of the above.

questions.stem: The audio management system allows the flight crew to use:

explanation.confuseWith: 2 hours is how much the CVR keeps; the 5-minute figures are its automatic start and stop timers on the ground.
explanation.text: False. The CVR retains the last 2 hours of recording, not 60 minutes. It is a crash-protected four-track recorder in the aft part of the fuselage, fitted with an underwater locating beacon. It takes its audio from an area microphone behind the overhead panel and, through a hot-mike function, straight from each crew microphone even when no push-to-talk switch is pressed.

options.text: True.
False

questions.stem: Only the last 60 minutes of recording are retained by the CVR.

explanation.confuseWith: The attendant light flashes for a call from the cabin crew; MECH is the call from the ground crew.
explanation.text: False. A flashing MECH light on the ACP means the ground crew is calling the cockpit: the mechanic has pressed COCKPIT CALL on the external power panel, and a buzzer sounds as well. The light goes out after 60 s if nobody resets it on the ACP.

options.text: True.
False.

questions.stem: The flashing amber MECH light indicates that the interphone system is faulty.

explanation.confuseWith: One engine is enough; the CVR does not wait for both engines to run.
explanation.text: 5 and 1. On the ground the CVR records for the first 5 minutes after the aircraft electrical network is powered, and it records whenever one engine is running. It goes on in flight and until 5 minutes after the last engine is shut down. Outside these periods on the ground, the crew can start it with the GND CTL pushbutton.

questions.stem: The cockpit voice recorder will automatically operate on the ground for _______ minutes after electrical power is supplied to the airplane; or when at least _______ engine is operating.

explanation.confuseWith: The external horn comes from the MECH pushbutton on the overhead panel; the ACP key only chooses the flight interphone for talking.
explanation.text: Pressing the INT transmission key, which carries the MECH light, selects the flight interphone for transmission. The pilot then speaks by pressing a push-to-talk switch, such as the sidestick radio switch, or by setting the INT/RAD switch to RAD. The ground crew hears him through the FLT INT jack on the maintenance panel at the nose landing gear. Calls with the cabin crew go through the CAB key instead.

options.text: The flight interphone channel is selected for transmission via the ACP RAD switch or the side stick radio selector.
The cabin interphone channel is selected for transmission via the ACP RAD switch
You can speak to the ground mechanic via the handset
The mechanic will hear the external horn sound.

questions.stem: With the INT transmission key on the Audio Control Panel pressed:

explanation.confuseWith: The 5 min after power-up is a short window, not continuous recording while the aircraft is powered.
explanation.text: In automatic mode the CVR records on the ground for only the first 5 min after the network is powered, then stops until an engine is started. It then records with an engine running, throughout the flight, and for 5 min after the last engine shutdown. To record at another time on the ground, the crew presses the GND CTL pb on the overhead panel.

options.text: No: in automatic mode it records only in flight
No: on the ground it records only briefly after power-up
Yes: it records whenever the network is powered
Yes: it records until the first engine start

questions.stem: On the ground, engines stopped, the aircraft has been powered for 10 min and GND CTL is not pressed. Is the CVR recording?

explanation.confuseWith: The cargo doors always use the yellow system, with a hand pump as back-up; no other system takes over after engine start.
explanation.text: The forward and aft cargo doors are opened and closed by the yellow hydraulic system. At the door service panel, holding the selector valve lever runs the yellow electric pump, which stops when the lever returns to neutral. The locks that hold the door open or closed are mechanical. If the electric pump or the electrical supply fails, a hand pump at the yellow ground service panel can still move the door, with two people working it.

options.text: The blue electric pump.
The yellow hydraulic system before engine start and the green hydraulic system after engine start.
The yellow hydraulic system.
The blue hydraulic system before engine start and the green hydraulic system after engine start.

questions.stem: The cargo doors are powered by:

explanation.confuseWith: The slide is carried on the door itself and anchored at floor level, not on the fuselage underside or above the door.
explanation.text: With the arming lever at ARMED, the slide is hooked to brackets in the floor at each side of the doorway. Opening the door from inside then makes the slide, stowed in a container on the inboard lower part of the door, inflate and deploy by itself. If the inflation bottle does not fire on its own, a crew member can release it by hand with its valve. An opening from outside cancels the arming of both door and slide.

options.text: To the brackets on the underside of the fuselage.
To the brackets above the door.
To the floor brackets on both sides of the door.
All of the above

questions.stem: When the slide arming lever, on the emergency opening system, is in the ARMED position, where is the slide connected?

explanation.confuseWith: The arming lever belongs to the passenger doors, not to the overwing exits.
explanation.text: No. Each overwing exit slide is permanently armed, so there is no arming lever to set. Removing the handle cover already lights the handle and the SLIDE ARMED indicator, which shows that the slide will deploy when the exit is thrown out. The passenger doors are different: each has a slide arming lever, and opening a door from outside disarms it.

options.text: No, they are always armed
Yes, each exit has a slide arming lever

questions.stem: Do the overwing emergency exit slides have to be armed with a lever before flight?

explanation.confuseWith: DC BUS 2 feeds the DC BAT BUS only after a failure on the number 1 side, and then after a 5 s delay.
explanation.text: In normal operation the DC BAT BUS is on the number 1 side: TR 1 supplies DC BUS 1, the DC BAT BUS and the DC ESS BUS, while TR 2 supplies only DC BUS 2. The DC buses are linked by automatic switching. If AC BUS 1 is lost, DC BUS 2 picks up DC BUS 1 and the DC BAT BUS by itself after 5 s. The batteries themselves join the DC BAT BUS only when they need charging.

options.text: DC BUS 2
DC BUS 1 and DC BUS 2
DC bus 1 through a DC tie control relay.
DC bus 2 through a DC tie control relay.

questions.stem: The BATTERY BUS is normally powered by:

explanation.confuseWith: The BAT pushbuttons go to AUTO only after the voltage check; with 25.5 V or less a charging cycle of about 20 minutes on external power comes first.
explanation.text: Both BAT pushbuttons must be checked OFF before the battery voltages are read. The batteries stay permanently connected to their hot buses, so the overhead voltmeters read them with the pushbuttons off. The check is for an aircraft that has had no electrical power for 6 h or more: a voltage above 25.5 V means a charge above 50 %, and the pushbuttons then go to AUTO.

options.text: You have to check that the external power is on.
You have to ensure that at least one battery is on.
You have to ensure that both batteries are on.
You have to verify that both batteries are off.

questions.stem: You enter a dark cockpit, what action is necessary before checking the battery voltages?

explanation.confuseWith: Alternate law is the law of this configuration with the gear up; extending the gear changes it to direct law.
explanation.text: Direct law. In the emergency electrical configuration the flight controls are in alternate law without protections, and once the landing gear is extended they change to direct law in pitch and roll. The ECAM status page reminds the crew of this. Autopilot and autothrust are lost, so the approach is flown by hand, at no less than the minimum RAT speed of 140 kt.

options.text: Backup.
Direct.
Alternate.
Backup or alternate

questions.stem: While operating on Emergency Electrical Power with the landing gear lowered which of the following control laws is in effect?

explanation.confuseWith: Selecting GEN OFF then ON resets the generator fault circuit; it does nothing for a disconnected IDG.
explanation.text: No: once disconnected, an IDG cannot be reconnected by the crew. Pressing the guarded IDG pushbutton separates the drive from its shaft, and only maintenance personnel can reconnect it. The generator on that side stays lost, and the APU generator, if available, or the other engine generator takes over its buses automatically.

options.text: Yes, but only after contacting maintenance control.
Yes, push and hold the IDG pb until the GEN fault light is no longer illuminated.
No, it is not possible.
Yes, by selecting the GEN pushbutton OFF then ON.

questions.stem: Can you reconnect an IDG in flight?

explanation.confuseWith: 50 kt is the AC ESS BUS threshold; 100 kt is the speed below which the batteries reconnect to the DC BAT BUS.
explanation.text: True: when only the batteries remain and the speed is above 50 kt, battery 1 feeds the AC ESS BUS through the static inverter, which turns its DC into single-phase AC. Battery 2 feeds the DC ESS BUS at the same time. On the ground under 50 kt the AC ESS BUS is dropped, and the static inverter then feeds only the AC STAT INV bus.

options.text: True.
False.

questions.stem: The AC Essential bus is powered by the battery at speed above 50 kt.

explanation.confuseWith: The static inverter feeds the AC ESS BUS only when the batteries are the last source, not after a single AC bus failure.
explanation.text: AC BUS 2 takes over the AC ESS BUS when AC BUS 1 fails. The crew does it with the AC ESS FEED pushbutton, or it happens by itself on aircraft with automatic AC ESS FEED switching. The ESS TR then supplies the DC ESS BUS, and DC BUS 2 picks up DC BUS 1 and the DC BAT BUS after 5 s. The emergency sources are kept for the loss of both main AC buses.

options.text: Emer Gen.
The RAT
Static Inverter
AC Bus 2

questions.stem: If AC Bus 1 fails the AC ESS bus is supplied by:

explanation.confuseWith: The ATT HDG selector at CAPT 3 keeps IR 3 supplied; nothing keeps IR 2 after the 5 min.
explanation.text: Only IR 1 is kept in the emergency electrical configuration. IR 2 and IR 3 keep running for 5 min after the main generators fail and are then lost. If the crew sets the ATT HDG selector to CAPT 3 so that IR 3 replaces IR 1, IR 3 stays supplied. The same applies with the emergency generator running and on batteries only, in flight and on the ground.

options.text: Both are lost 5 min after the main generators fail; IR 3 stays supplied if ATT HDG is at CAPT 3
IR 2 stays supplied; IR 3 is lost at once
Both are lost at once; IR 3 returns if ATT HDG is set to CAPT 3
Both stay supplied as long as the emergency generator runs

questions.stem: ELEC EMER CONFIG with the emergency generator running. What happens to IR 2 and IR 3?

explanation.confuseWith: The standby indicator is the usual back-up, but here it is the one whose probe has no heat.
explanation.text: In the emergency electrical configuration the captain's pitot keeps its heat, but the standby probe is not de-iced. In icing the standby probe may ice up and read wrong, so the ECAM tells the crew to disregard the standby airspeed when it disagrees with the CM1 PFD. The CM1 PFD stays available and is fed by ADR 1, the only ADR left in this configuration.

options.text: The CM1 PFD: the standby probe is not de-iced
Neither: apply UNRELIABLE SPEED INDICATION at once
The standby indicator: it is independent of the ADIRUs
The one closer to the expected pitch and thrust

questions.stem: ELEC EMER CONFIG in icing conditions. The CM1 PFD and the standby airspeed indicator disagree. Which does the crew believe?

explanation.confuseWith: The BAT pb controls the link to the DC BAT BUS, not the link to the hot bus, which is permanent.
explanation.text: Each main battery has a normal capacity of 23 Ah, and its link to the hot bus has no switch in it, so the hot buses keep their supply even with the BAT pbs OFF. The BAT pb controls the battery charge limiter, which closes the battery line contactor to the DC BAT BUS only in set cases, such as an APU start or a charge when the voltage drops below 26.5 V.

options.text: 40 Ah each, permanently connected to the DC BAT BUS
23 Ah each, permanently connected to their hot buses
23 Ah each, connected to their hot buses only with BAT at AUTO
23 Ah each, connected only in the emergency configuration

questions.stem: Which statement about the two main batteries is correct?

explanation.confuseWith: BUS TIE goes back to AUTO later, before the APU start, so the APU generator can take a channel.
explanation.text: The first reset recycles the generators one after the other with the channels still linked. If none comes back, BUS TIE goes OFF, which segregates the two generator channels, so that each generator is tried again on its own channel. When any of these resets works, both FACs are reset. BUS TIE is set back to AUTO later in the procedure, before the APU start.

options.text: To shed the galleys and commercial loads
To separate the two generator channels
To isolate the emergency generator from the batteries
To connect the APU generator to both sides

questions.stem: ELEC EMER CONFIG: the first generator reset has failed. Why does the procedure set BUS TIE to OFF before trying again?

explanation.confuseWith: FLX and MCT share one detent; they are not two separate positions.
explanation.text: Six positions. Forward of idle there are the IDLE stop, the CL detent, the FLX/MCT detent and the TO/GA stop. Behind idle, once the reverse lever is lifted to unlock it, come the REV IDLE detent and the maximum reverse stop, which gives the MREV rating. The FADEC reads where the lever is and sets the thrust rating limit to match.

options.text: There are 6 thrust levers positions: TO/GA, MCT, FLEX, CL, IDLE and REV IDLE.
There are 6 thrust levers positions: TO/GA, FLX/MCT, CL, IDLE, REV IDLE and MREV.
There are 4 thrust levers positions: TO/GA, FLX/MCT, CL, IDLE.
There are 5 thrust levers positions: TO/GA, FLX/MCT, CL, IDLE and REV IDLE.

questions.stem: How many thrust lever positions are there, and how are they labeled?

explanation.confuseWith: The A/THR status (armed or active) is on line 3 of column 5; column 1 shows the mode.
explanation.text: Column 1 of the FMA is the A/THR messages and modes column. With the A/THR active, line 1 shows the engaged A/THR mode, such as SPEED or THR CLB. With the A/THR armed, the first two lines show the manual thrust in use, such as MAN TOGA or MAN FLX. Whether the A/THR is armed or active is shown elsewhere, on line 3 of column 5.

options.text: If A/THR is off, armed, or active.
The mode of the A/THR in use when A/THR is armed or active.
Amber caution messages.
The thrust indication.

questions.stem: The left column, first line of the FMA is used to indicate:

explanation.confuseWith: Igniters A and B are not tied to one engine; each engine has both, and the FADEC alternates them.
explanation.text: Yes. In an automatic ground start the FADEC powers only one igniter for the first start attempt, and it alternates the igniters (and the channels) from one start to the next. So engine 2 may use igniter B on one start and igniter A on the next; the ENG SD page shows which igniter is in use. Both igniters are used in a manual start and in flight.

options.text: Yes, igniter A is only used for engine anti-ice.
No, normally both igniters are used for all engine starts.
Yes, igniter B is always used for ENG 2 start.
Yes, igniters are used alternately for engine start.

questions.stem: During the automatic start sequence of ENG 2, you notice that only igniter B is powered. Is it normal?

explanation.confuseWith: The order is green then yellow: engine 1 on green, engine 2 on yellow, never the other way round.
explanation.text: Green for engine 1 (left) and yellow for engine 2 (right). The translating sleeves or blocker doors of each reverser are moved by hydraulic power from that system, under the control of the engine's own FADEC. Both engine types use the same split, and each reverser works independently of the other.

options.text: Green - Yellow.
Yellow - Blue.
Yellow - Green.
Blue - Green.

questions.stem: For reverser actuation, the left engine uses ____ hydraulic system pressure and the right engine uses _____ hydraulic system pressure.

explanation.confuseWith: An automatic start uses one igniter for the first attempt; a manual start uses both.
explanation.text: At ENG MASTER ON in a manual start, the FADEC opens the HP fuel valve and powers both igniters, so the crew checks igniters A and B on and the fuel flow rising, and starts the chrono for the light-up. The fuel used indication resets on the ground at the engine start. N2 has already been rising since the start valve opened.

options.text: The fuel used is reset, fuel flow is indicated and IGNITION message on the E/WD.
The fuel flow is reset, an igniter is powered and fuel used is indicated.
The fuel used is reset, both igniters are powered and fuel flow is indicated.
The fuel used is reset, both igniters are powered and N2 is increasing.

questions.stem: You are in the middle of a manual engine start. What are you looking for when you select ENG MASTER 2 ON?

explanation.confuseWith: The trigger is the FLAPS lever position, not the landing gear or a radio height.
explanation.text: Approach idle is a higher idle used as soon as the FLAPS lever leaves 0. It keeps the engine spinning fast enough to reach go-around thrust quickly if needed. Approach idle depends on the aircraft altitude, not on the bleed demand. With the flaps lever at 0 the FADEC uses modulated idle, which follows the bleed demand and the ambient conditions. Reverse idle on the ground is slightly above forward idle.

options.text: When the FLAPS lever is not at 0, to give more bleed air for the wing anti-ice
Below 1 000 ft RA, so the engine can accelerate quickly to go-around thrust
When the FLAPS lever is not at 0, so the engine can accelerate quickly to go-around thrust
When the gear is down, so the engine can accelerate quickly to go-around thrust

questions.stem: In flight, when does the FADEC select approach idle, and why?

explanation.confuseWith: A red SD pressure with no alert is the faulty transducer case; here it is the alert that the SD does not confirm.
explanation.text: The procedure starts with a check of the oil pressure on the ENG SD page, because the alert and the indication can come from different sensors. Only if the pressure there is below the limit does the crew set the thrust lever to idle and the master lever OFF. The opposite case, a red pressure on the SD without the alert, points to a faulty transducer, and the engine may keep running.

options.text: Thrust lever 1 to IDLE and ENG MASTER 1 OFF at once
Thrust lever 1 to IDLE, and a restart after 30 s
ENG MASTER 1 OFF, and the ENG FIRE pb pushed
No shutdown while the SD pressure stays above the limit

questions.stem: ENG 1 OIL LO PR warning in cruise. The PM checks the ENG SD page: the oil pressure of engine 1 is above the red limit. What does the procedure require?

explanation.confuseWith: ENG MAN START ON opens the start valve only with the ENG MODE selector out of NORM; CRANK is the position meant for a dry crank.
explanation.text: A dry crank turns the engine with the starter but without fuel or ignition, to blow fuel vapour out after a failed start. CRANK on the ENG MODE selector with ENG MAN START ON opens the start valve, and with the ENG MASTER lever left OFF the HP fuel valve stays shut and the igniters are not powered. Setting ENG MAN START back to OFF ends the cranking.

options.text: ENG MODE to NORM, ENG MAN START ON, ENG MASTER OFF
ENG MODE to CRANK, ENG MAN START ON, ENG MASTER OFF
ENG MODE to CRANK, ENG MAN START OFF, ENG MASTER OFF
ENG MODE to CRANK, ENG MASTER ON

questions.stem: After an unsuccessful start on the ground, how does the crew select a dry crank of the engine?

explanation.confuseWith: Residual cabin pressure is shown by a different light, the red CABIN PRESSURE warning light, which flashes.
explanation.text: The slide is still armed. A white SLIDE ARMED light in the door's observation window comes on steadily when the slide arming lever is at ARMED and someone starts to lift the door control handle. It warns that, if the handle goes on up, the door will open in emergency mode and the slide will deploy. Both door lights can be seen from inside and outside the aircraft.

options.text: There is residual pressure in the cabin.
The ramp is not correctly positioned.
The slide is still armed.
Somebody is trying to open the door from outside.

questions.stem: You want to open the cabin door, whilst lifting the control handle the white light illuminates. What does it mean?

explanation.confuseWith: The right-hand dome light, not the left, is kept on batteries.
explanation.text: Only the right-hand dome light works when the batteries are the only source of electrical power. The cockpit has two dimmable dome lights for general lighting, and the left one is not kept on batteries. The instrument panels have their own integral and flood lighting, all with adjustable brightness, and spot and flood lights cover the work surfaces and the side consoles.

options.text: Neither dome light
Both dome lights, at reduced brightness
The right-hand dome light only
The left-hand dome light only

questions.stem: The aircraft is on batteries only. Which cockpit dome light still works?

explanation.confuseWith: The avionics bay does have smoke detection: one detector in its air extraction duct, which lights the GEN 1 LINE SMOKE light.
explanation.text: True: the avionics bay is watched for smoke, but it has no fixed extinguishing system. The aircraft detects fire in the engines and the APU, and smoke in the cargo holds, the lavatories and the avionics bay. Fixed extinguishing is fitted for the engines, the APU, the cargo holds and the lavatory waste bins. Portable extinguishers are carried in the cockpit and in the cabin.

options.text: True.
False.

questions.stem: The avionics compartment is the only area where there is no fire extinguishing system installed.

explanation.confuseWith: In flight on batteries only, APU fire detection and automatic extinguishing are inoperative.
explanation.text: Yes: on the ground the APU fire protection still works on batteries, including the automatic shutdown and discharge. An APU fire detected on the ground makes the APU stop by itself, and the bottle discharges automatically 3 seconds after the warning. On batteries only, APU fire detection and automatic extinguishing are lost in flight, but both come back once the speed is below 100 kt.

options.text: Yes, the APU will initiate an auto shutdown and discharge the extinguishing agent.
No, but the APU will initiate an auto shutdown.
No, automatic fire protection is only available if AC power is available.
Yes, but the agent must be discharged manually.

questions.stem: When the aircraft is on the ground and the APU is started on battery power only, is fire protection available?

explanation.confuseWith: A bottle that has lost its pressure in the normal way shows the amber DISCH light on the APU AGENT pushbutton, in the cockpit.
explanation.text: A missing red disc means the APU bottle has released its agent overboard through its overpressure relief. The disc sits outside, at the rear of the fuselage, and the walkaround of the APU area checks that it is still in place.

options.text: This is normal indication, the red APU thermal plug only appears if the APU halon cylinder is low.
An APU fire agent thermal discharge has occurred.
An external fire discharge has been activated.
One of the engine fire bottles has discharged overboard.

questions.stem: What is indicated by a missing red APU thermal plug during an exterior preflight?

explanation.confuseWith: Both FAULT lights also come on after a ventilation controller failure, so it is the GEN 1 LINE SMOKE light that points to smoke.
explanation.text: Both FAULT lights come on. When the single detector in the avionics extraction duct senses smoke for more than 5 seconds, it lights the GEN 1 LINE SMOKE light and the FAULT lights in both the BLOWER and the EXTRACT pushbuttons on the VENTILATION panel. With both pushbuttons then set to OVRD, cooling air from the air conditioning is sent overboard and the blower fan stops.

options.text: The BLOWER and EXTRACT push button FAULT lights will be illuminated.
Only the BLOWER FAULT light will be illuminated.
Only the EXTRACT FAULT light will be illuminated.
No FAULT light will be illuminated on the VENTILATION panel.

questions.stem: In conjunction with illumination of the GEN 1 LINE SMOKE light and MASTER CAUT light:

explanation.confuseWith: The engine fire extinguisher works on a fire outside the core; a tailpipe fire is inside the gas path.
explanation.text: Pushing the ENG FIRE pushbutton removes the FADEC power, which stops the dry crank sequence. A tailpipe fire is fuel burning inside the engine core, so the cure is to stop the fuel flow and blow the remaining fuel out by motoring the engine. The fire agent would not help either, because it does not reach a fire inside the engine. External agents are kept as a last resort, as they can badly corrode the engine.

options.text: It discharges the fire agent automatically
It shuts off the APU bleed needed for motoring
It reopens the LP fuel valve of that engine
It cuts the FADEC supply, so the engine cannot be motored

questions.stem: Engine tailpipe fire on the ground. Why must the crew not push the ENG FIRE pushbutton?

explanation.confuseWith: One detector alone is enough only if its partner is inoperative.
explanation.text: Each cavity has two detectors, one on each loop, and the warning normally needs both of them to see smoke. If one detector is inoperative, the other is enough on its own. Smoke at one detector of a healthy pair, or a time delay, is not part of the logic. With the warning, cargo ventilation, where fitted, is isolated: the isolation valves close and the extraction fan stops.

options.text: One detector sees smoke for more than 60 s
Any one of its detectors sees smoke, even with both working
Both its detectors see smoke, or one if the other is failed
Detectors in two different cavities see smoke

questions.stem: In a cargo compartment, when does smoke in one ceiling cavity trigger the cargo smoke warning?

explanation.confuseWith: ELAC 1 is the normal aileron computer and only the backup for pitch; ELAC 2 normally flies the elevators and the THS.
explanation.text: ELAC 2 is the normal pitch computer: it commands the elevators and the THS. The left and right elevators are then driven by green and yellow hydraulic jacks, and the THS by the first of its three electric motors. If ELAC 2 or its hydraulics fail, pitch passes to ELAC 1, and with both ELACs lost, SEC 1 or SEC 2 takes over.

options.text: SEC 1
FAC 1
ELAC 2
ELAC 1

questions.stem: What computer normally commands the operation of the elevators and horizontal stabilizer?

explanation.confuseWith: Staying in the last position is what a spoiler does after a hydraulic failure, not after the loss of its computer.
explanation.text: The spoilers of that computer retract automatically. Each SEC drives its own spoilers: SEC 3 spoiler 2, SEC 1 spoilers 3 and 4, SEC 2 spoiler 5. A spoiler that loses its electrical control, or shows a fault, is driven back to zero, and the symmetric surface on the other wing is inhibited. A spoiler keeps its deflection only when its hydraulic pressure is lost.

options.text: The affected spoilers automatically retract.
All spoilers automatically retract.
The affected spoilers remains in the last commanded position.
The affected spoilers go to the damping mode.

questions.stem: If electrical power to a SEC fails:

explanation.confuseWith: Alternate is the yaw law that goes with pitch alternate law; roll itself is direct.
explanation.text: Direct: whenever pitch is in alternate law, roll follows the roll direct law, in which the sidestick sets the aileron and spoiler positions directly. Yaw goes to alternate law (yaw damping only, limited to 5° of rudder) or to mechanical control. Bank angle protection is not provided. In roll direct law the roll rate is about 30° per second in clean configuration.

options.text: Direct
Normal
Alternate
Mechanical

questions.stem: With the aircraft in Pitch Alternate Law, roll is in _____ Law.

explanation.confuseWith: The limit covers any slat or flap extension, not only full flaps.
explanation.text: 20 000 ft is the maximum operating altitude with the slats or the flaps extended. The limit matters when slats or flaps are jammed: a diversion must then be flown at or below 20 000 ft. Likewise, the stall recovery procedure selects flaps 1 only when clean and below that altitude.

options.text: Max altitude for extension is 20, 000 ft.
Max altitude for extension is 22, 000 ft.
Max altitude for extension is 25, 000 ft
Max altitude for extension is 27, 000 ft.

questions.stem: Which altitude limitation is associated with high lift devices?

explanation.confuseWith: Losing hydraulic pressure is different: the spoiler then holds its position instead of retracting.
explanation.text: True: each spoiler is moved by a single servojack, on one hydraulic system, controlled by one SEC. If that computer fails, the spoiler retracts and its partner on the other wing is inhibited. The other surfaces have backups: the ailerons and elevators have two jacks and more than one computer each (the elevators pass from ELAC 2 to ELAC 1, then to SEC 1 or SEC 2), and the rudder has three jacks and two FACs.

options.text: True.
False.

questions.stem: The spoiler panels are the only flight control surfaces with no redundant control.

explanation.confuseWith: 33° is the bank the aircraft returns to when the stick is released, not the maximum reachable bank.
explanation.text: 67° is the most the bank can reach with full lateral stick in normal law. Up to 33° the aircraft holds the bank with the stick at neutral; beyond 33° bank angle protection gives positive spiral stability, so the crew must hold the stick to stay there, and auto trim stops. With the angle of attack protection active, the limit drops to 45°, and with high speed protection to 40°.

questions.stem: In normal law, what is the maximum bank angle you can reach with the side stick fully deflected?

explanation.confuseWith: A short press gives priority only while held; the lock that lasts after release needs the 40 s press.
explanation.text: True: a pilot keeps the takeover pushbutton on his own sidestick pressed, and after 40 s the other sidestick is deactivated. It stays deactivated after release until a pilot presses a takeover pushbutton again, so its own pilot can recover it by pressing his. A red arrow lights in front of the pilot who lost authority. A sidestick deactivated on the ground triggers a CONFIG SIDESTICK FAULT at take-off power.

options.text: True.
False.

questions.stem: To disable a side-stick, you have to depress the take-over button on the active stick. Holding the button down for 40 seconds will electrically lock the other stick out until either pilot presses a take-over button again.

explanation.confuseWith: Managed speed and ground speed mini are the normal choice; with jammed slats or flaps the speed stays selected.
explanation.text: With a jammed surface, the FMS approach speed does not match the real configuration, so the procedure asks the crew to decelerate to the VAPP they calculated and keep the selected speed. The PFD still helps: the overspeed alert and VLS follow the actual slat and flap position. The autopilot is not used below 500 ft AGL. During the configuration the speed is selected at VFE NEXT − 5 kt before each lever step.

options.text: Managed speed down to 500 ft, then selected
Selected speed down to 500 ft, then managed
Managed speed, for the ground speed mini function
Selected speed, kept until landing, at the calculated VAPP

questions.stem: LANDING WITH SLATS OR FLAPS JAMMED: the landing configuration is reached on final. Which speed mode is used down to landing?

explanation.confuseWith: The aircraft does not flare by itself in manual flight: the system lowers the nose, and the pilot's gentle pull makes the flare.
explanation.text: Passing 50 ft RA the trim stops and flare mode takes over, close to a direct stick-to-elevator relationship. The attitude held at 50 ft becomes the pitch reference. Passing 30 ft, the system starts to reduce that reference towards −2° nose down over about 8 s, which gives the landing a conventional feel. The pilot therefore makes a gentle nose-up input to flare.

options.text: It lowers the pitch reference to −2° over 8 s, so the pilot must pull gently to flare
It raises the pitch to +2° over 8 s, flaring the aircraft by itself
It lowers the pitch reference to −2° at once, and the THS trims nose down
It keeps the 50 ft attitude until touchdown, so no input is needed

questions.stem: Normal law, manual landing. What does flare mode do to the pitch attitude as the aircraft descends through 30 ft?

explanation.confuseWith: Losing the PFD protection strips does not mean the protections are lost; only their display is.
