explanation.text: The FCDCs gather ELAC and SEC data and pass it on to the displays and the maintenance system. With both lost, the ELACs and SECs keep flying in normal law, but the F/CTL page data, the flight control ECAM warnings, the bank and pitch limits and the Vα prot and Vα max strips on the PFD are gone. The crew therefore watches the flight control panel on the overhead.

options.text: Direct law at once, with the F/CTL page still available
Normal law stays, and all PFD speeds remain as usual
Normal law stays; F/CTL indications and PFD protection speeds are lost
Alternate law, with the protections lost and the PFD speeds kept

questions.stem: F/CTL FCDC 1+2 FAULT. What happens to the flight control laws?

explanation.confuseWith: No hydraulic control puts both jacks in damping; no electrical control puts them in centring.
explanation.text: Both jacks switch automatically to centring mode, in which hydraulics hold the jack in the neutral position. Each elevator has two servojacks with three modes: active, damping and centring. Normally one jack is active and the other damps. If the active jack fails, the damped one takes over. Damping mode for both jacks is the answer to the opposite case, when neither jack is controlled hydraulically.

options.text: Both go to centring mode
Both lock at their last position
Both go to damping mode
One stays active, the other damps

questions.stem: Neither servojack of an elevator is controlled electrically any more. What mode do the two jacks take?

explanation.confuseWith: On aircraft where the centre tank transfers its fuel to the wings through valves, centre fuel can still be used by gravity; with centre tank pumps it cannot.
explanation.text: On aircraft with centre tank pumps, only the wing tanks can feed the engines by gravity. Pump pressure normally holds the suction valves of the inner tank pumps shut; if those pumps fail, the valves open and the engines draw fuel by gravity. Outer tank fuel reaches the inner tank through the transfer valves, which open at the inner tank low level. The centre tank pumps have no suction or by-pass valve, so centre fuel becomes unusable.

options.text: Outer cell of the wing tanks, inner cell of the wing tanks, and/or center tank.
Inner cell of the wing tanks, and center tank.
Outer cell of the wing tanks, and inner cell of the wing tanks.
The center tank only.

questions.stem: On aircraft with centre tank pumps, from which tanks will fuel gravity feed?

explanation.confuseWith: In MAN the pumps run without these stops, and the crew must switch them OFF when the centre tank is empty.
explanation.text: Both statements hold in AUTO with the CTR TK PUMP pushbuttons ON. The pumps run for about 2 min at engine start, and otherwise only while the slats are retracted. They stop when the slats are extended, and 5 min after the centre tank low level is reached. Each pump also stops while its inner tank is full, and runs again once about 500 kg of that tank has been used.

options.text: Will operate for a short period after the first engine MASTER switch is selected ON and while slats are retracted.
Will stop when the slats are extended, and five minutes after the centre tank low level is reached.
Both are correct.
Neither is correct.

questions.stem: With fuel in the centre tank, the CTR TK MODE SEL push button selected to AUTO and the CTR TK PUMP push buttons ON (lights out), the centre tank pumps:

explanation.confuseWith: Closing the crossfeed to keep each side separate is the fuel leak rule, where a leak must not affect both sides.
explanation.text: With low level in both inner tanks the aircraft must land as soon as possible. If the centre tank is not empty, its fuel is sent to the wings or fed directly, and all the wing pumps are set on. With no leak, the crossfeed is opened so that both engines can use the fuel left in either wing. If the engines are fed by gravity, the crossfeed is set off again, as in the gravity fuel feeding procedure.

options.text: ON in every case, including gravity feeding
OFF, so that each engine keeps its own tank
ON only if the centre tank is empty
ON, but OFF again if the engines are fed by gravity

questions.stem: FUEL L + R WING TK LO LVL with no fuel leak. What does the procedure say about the crossfeed?

explanation.confuseWith: Slowing down lowers the TAT and makes the fuel colder, not warmer.
explanation.text: The procedure suggests descending, flying faster, or both, to raise the TAT. Fuel temperature slowly moves toward the TAT, and a lower level (below the tropopause) or a higher Mach gives a higher TAT. The alert comes when the fuel is at about -43 °C. In flight it is for crew awareness; on the ground it delays the take-off.

options.text: Climb to a higher flight level to raise the TAT
Reduce the Mach number to lower the fuel flow
Descend and/or increase the Mach number to raise the TAT
Open the crossfeed to mix warmer fuel

questions.stem: FUEL L OUTER TK LO TEMP in cruise. What does the procedure suggest?

explanation.confuseWith: Crossfeed ON belongs to the case above FL 150.
explanation.text: Above FL 150 the crossfeed is opened so that the right tank pumps feed both engines. Below FL 150 the procedure closes it, and as long as it stays closed engine 1 is fed by gravity from the left tank. The crew then follows the GRAVITY FUEL FEEDING procedure and avoids negative g load, which could interrupt a gravity feed.

options.text: Crossfeed ON; engine 1 is fed by the right tank pumps
Crossfeed OFF; engine 1 is fed by gravity from its own tank
Crossfeed OFF; engine 1 is fed by the centre tank pumps
Crossfeed ON; both engines are fed by gravity

questions.stem: FUEL L TK PUMP 1+2 LO PR, no fuel leak, below FL 150. What does the procedure do with the crossfeed, and how is engine 1 fed?

questions.context: On aircraft with centre tank pumps.

explanation.confuseWith: MAN mode lets the crew run the centre pumps by hand; it does not lift the take-off prohibition.
explanation.text: False: take-off on centre tank feeding is prohibited, whatever the pump mode. That is why, at AUTO, the centre tank pumps stop when the slats are extended and run again only once the slats are retracted, apart from their 2 min run at each engine start. The engines are then fed from the wing tanks during take-off. MAN mode gives the crew control of the pumps, not an exemption from the limitation.

options.text: True
False

questions.stem: Take-off with the engines fed from the centre tank is permitted if the centre tank pumps are selected to MAN.

explanation.confuseWith: 3 to 5 minutes is the time at about FL 250; at FL 350 it is under a minute.
explanation.text: About 30 seconds to 1 minute. This is the time a person can still act sensibly, for example put on an oxygen mask, before hypoxia takes over; unconsciousness follows soon after. It shrinks quickly with altitude, from 3 to 5 minutes at FL 250 to about 15 to 20 seconds at FL 400, and a rapid decompression cuts it further. So the crew puts the masks on first, at once.

options.text: 3 to 5 minutes
5 to 10 minutes
10 to 15 seconds
30 seconds to 1 minute

questions.stem: After a sudden loss of cabin pressure at FL 350, about how long is the time of useful consciousness without oxygen?

explanation.confuseWith: The PTU moves pressure between green and yellow, never fluid.
explanation.text: False: hydraulic fluid can never pass from one system to another. The A320 has three hydraulic systems (blue, green and yellow), each with a reservoir of its own, and all three run continuously at 3 000 PSI. The PTU lets the green and yellow systems pressurise each other, but it transfers power, not fluid. A leak in one system therefore cannot drain another.

options.text: True
False

questions.stem: Fluid can be transferred between hydraulic systems.

explanation.confuseWith: The valve closes above 264 kt; below 260 kt the supply still stays cut until the gear lever is selected down.
explanation.text: Above 264 kt the gear safety valve shuts off green pressure to the landing gear automatically, so the gear and doors cannot be moved at high speed. The green system normally powers all gear and door actuation, sequenced electrically by the LGCIUs. Once cut, the supply stays cut even below 260 kt while the gear lever is up; selecting the gear down restores it.

questions.stem: Beyond which speed is the landing gear isolated from hydraulic pressure by its safety valve?

explanation.confuseWith: The automatic trigger is electrical (both main AC buses lost above 100 kt), never a hydraulic failure.
explanation.text: Only by hand. The RAT extends automatically only when both main AC buses are unpowered with the speed above 100 kt, and it then also drives the emergency generator. A hydraulic failure, even of two systems, does not extend it. To get blue pressure from the RAT, the crew presses the guarded RAT MAN ON pushbutton.

options.text: Automatically with the failure of both the green and blue hydraulic systems.
Automatically with the failure of both the green and yellow hydraulic systems.
Only when the guarded RAT MAN ON push button is selected by the crew.
When airspeed drops below 100 knots with the gear up.

questions.stem: For hydraulic system malfunctions, when will the RAT deploy?

explanation.confuseWith: Alternate braking uses the yellow system, so it remains after a green loss; normal braking is the one lost.
explanation.text: Losing the green system takes away reverser 1, landing gear retraction and normal braking, along with the autobrake, spoilers 1 and 5 and yaw damper 1. Braking is then on the yellow system, as alternate braking with anti-skid, and the slats and flaps move slowly. The gear can still be lowered by gravity. Reverser 2 belongs to the yellow side, so it stays available.

options.text: Reverser 1, gear retraction and alternate braking.
Reverser 1, gear retraction and normal braking.
Reverser 2, gear retraction and the cargo doors.
Reverser 2, gear retraction and normal braking.

questions.stem: If you lost the GREEN system, what equipment is lost?

explanation.confuseWith: The blue system has no engine pump, yet its reservoir is pressurised the same way, from engine 1 bleed air.
explanation.text: All three reservoirs are pressurised automatically with HP bleed air taken from engine 1. If that supply is too weak, the system takes air from the crossbleed duct instead. The air pressure on the fluid keeps the pump inlets fed, so that the pumps do not cavitate. This is why a low reservoir air pressure leads to the HYD RSVR LO AIR PR alert and possible loss of the system.

options.text: Cabin air through a pressure regulator in the hydraulic bay
Bleed air from the engine that drives each system's own pump
HP bleed air from engine 1, or from the crossbleed duct if that is too low
HP bleed air from engine 2, or from the APU if that is too low

questions.stem: What keeps the air pressure in the three hydraulic reservoirs?

explanation.confuseWith: The RAT pump is on the blue system only; green and yellow can back each other up only through the PTU.
explanation.text: Engine 1 drives the green pump, so the green system loses its pump. As green pressure falls, the difference with the yellow system soon passes 500 PSI, and the PTU starts by itself: yellow, driven by engine 2, then pressurises green. The PTU transfers power only; no fluid passes between the systems. The RAT cannot help green, because its pump serves the blue system alone.

options.text: Yellow; the yellow electric pump
Green; the PTU, powered by the yellow system
Green; the RAT, extended manually
Blue; the RAT, which deploys automatically

questions.stem: Engine 1 fails in flight. Which hydraulic system loses its engine-driven pump, and what can keep that system pressurised?

explanation.confuseWith: With both engines stopped the PTU can run even with the parking brake set, for example from the yellow electric pump.
explanation.text: No. On the ground the 500 PSI difference is not enough by itself: the PTU also needs both master levers at OFF, or both at ON, or the parking brake released with the nosewheel steering out of the towing position. With one engine running and the parking brake set, none of these holds, so the PTU stays inhibited. The first engine start keeps the PTU inhibited, and the second start tests it.

options.text: Yes, the pressure difference alone starts it
No, the PTU is inhibited in this configuration

questions.stem: On the ground only engine 1 is running and the parking brake is set. The green-yellow pressure difference exceeds 500 PSI. Does the PTU run?

explanation.confuseWith: The engine air intakes also get hot air, but from each engine's own high-pressure compressor, not from the pneumatic system.
explanation.text: Only the three outboard slats of each wing, slats 3, 4 and 5, are anti-iced with hot air. The pneumatic system feeds them through one valve per wing, and a single WING pushbutton on the overhead ANTI ICE panel works both valves. The flaps and the inner slats are not on the list of protected areas. The only other parts protected by hot air are the engine air intakes.

options.text: Slats
Flaps
Three outboard slats
Three inboard slats

questions.stem: The ______ on each wing are anti-iced with pneumatic bleed air.

explanation.confuseWith: The low-pressure trigger belongs to the wing light only; the engine light reacts to the valve position alone.
explanation.text: Both FAULT lights come on for a valve that disagrees with the selection, and both come on briefly while the valves move. Only the wing light has a third trigger: low pressure in the wing anti-ice supply. Each light comes with an ECAM caution. One WING pushbutton works both wing valves together, while each engine has its own pushbutton and valve.

options.text: Both indicate valve in transit, or valve position disagrees with selected position. Wing light also could indicate low pressure.
Both indicate low pressure, or valve position disagrees with selected position. Wing light might indicate valve in transit.
Both indicate valve in transit, or low pressure. Wing light also could indicate valve position disagrees with selected position.
Both indicate valve in transit, or overheat

questions.stem: What is the difference between the engine and wing anti-ice fault lights?

explanation.confuseWith: Window, probe and drain mast protection is electrical heating, not hot air.
explanation.text: Hot-air anti-ice covers only two areas: the engine air intakes and, on each wing, the three outboard slats of the leading edge. The slats, numbers 3, 4 and 5, take air from the pneumatic system, while each intake takes bleed from its own engine. The horizontal and vertical stabilisers are not among the protected areas. Everything else that is protected is heated electrically.

options.text: The engine nacelle’s and three outboard wing slats.
The engine nacelle’s, the horizontal stabilizer, and three outboard wing slats.
The engine nacelle’s, the horizontal stabilizer, the vertical stabilizer and three outboard wing slats.
The engine nacelle’s and all wing slats.

questions.stem: Anti-ice and de-icing protection is provided for:

explanation.confuseWith: The pushbuttons on the panel are for the optional rain repellent, not for the wipers.
explanation.text: Each wiper has its own rotary selector, so the two windshields are controlled separately. Each front windshield has one electric wiper with low and high speed, plus an intermittent sweep where that option is installed. Turned off, a wiper stops out of view. Rain repellent, where installed, also has one pushbutton for each side. The maximum speed for sweeping wipers is 230 kt.

options.text: Automatically when in heavy rain
By two individual pushbuttons
By one rotary selector for both windshields
By two individual rotary selectors

questions.stem: The electric windshield wipers are controlled:

explanation.confuseWith: The WING pb opens and closes both sides together; the leak protection closes only the affected side.
explanation.text: Only the right wing anti-ice valve closes. When a leak is detected, the valve on the affected side closes automatically, while the other wing keeps its hot air. At the same time the leak logic closes the engine 2 bleed valve and the crossbleed. The single WING pb sets both valves together in normal use, but the leak protection works on each side separately.

options.text: Both wing valves close, as the pb controls both sides
The right wing switches over to APU bleed air
The right valve stays open; only the bleed valve closes
The right valve closes; the left wing stays protected

questions.stem: In icing conditions with wing anti-ice ON, a leak is detected in the right wing. What happens to the wing anti-ice?

explanation.confuseWith: A cancelled caution is a white line on the STATUS page itself, not an arrow.
explanation.text: The arrow means the STATUS page holds more than fits on screen. It appears when the content overflows the left or right part of the page, and the crew presses CLR to scroll to the rest. The page itself sums up the aircraft state: limitations and procedures in blue, inoperative systems in amber, information in green, and cancelled cautions and maintenance status in white.

options.text: It is a reminder to land as soon as possible.
It indicates that there is a system page behind.
It means that there is more information to be seen.
It indicates that a cancelled caution is listed.

questions.stem: On a bottom of the STATUS page, what does the green arrow mean?

explanation.confuseWith: Two DMCs work normally; the third is a standby that the crew switches in.
explanation.text: Three identical DMCs are fitted. They take in data from the sensors and computers and process the data for the PFDs, NDs and both ECAM displays. In normal use DMC 1 serves the captain's side and DMC 2 the first officer's, while DMC 3 waits on standby and can replace either of them through the EIS DMC selector.

questions.stem: How many DMC’s are there?

explanation.confuseWith: CLR clears an alert from the E/WD but does not cancel it; only EMER CANC makes it a cancelled caution.
explanation.text: With the EMER CANC pushbutton. A caution cancelled this way loses its chime, MASTER CAUT lights and ECAM message until the flight ends, and the STATUS page then lists it in white as a cancelled caution. If the crew needs it back, holding the RCL pushbutton for more than 3 seconds recalls every alert cancelled this way.

options.text: By pressing the EMER CANC pushbutton.
By pressing the CLR key
By pressing the STS key
By pressing the ALL key.

questions.stem: How did the PNF cancel the caution for the NAV ILS 1 FAULT before calling the STATUS page on the ECP?

explanation.confuseWith: The two limits are not symmetrical: 73° in the north but 60° in the south.
explanation.text: North of 73° North or south of 60° South. In those regions the heading scale shows true heading instead of magnetic, and a true-heading label appears on the PFD and ND to tell the crew. Elsewhere the scale shows magnetic heading against the fixed yellow reference line, with the actual track as a small green diamond.

options.text: North of 73° North or South of 60° South
South of 73° North or North of 60° South.
North of 80° North or South of 73°South
North of 78° North or South of 78°South

questions.stem: When will the PFD Heading tape revert to TRUE heading?

explanation.confuseWith: DH + 100 ft is the amber threshold only when a DH has been entered and an FMGC is available to send it.
explanation.text: The radio height on the PFD normally changes colour relative to the decision height entered in the FMGC: amber from DH + 100 ft. With both FMGCs lost, no DH reaches the display, so a fixed threshold is used instead: green between 2 500 ft and 400 ft, amber at 400 ft and below. The same fixed rule applies when no DH has been entered at all.

options.text: At 1 000 ft RA and below
At 100 ft RA and below
At 400 ft RA and below
At DH + 100 ft and below

questions.stem: Both FMGCs have failed. On the approach, at what height does the radio height on the PFD turn amber?

explanation.confuseWith: The bird is fine for stabilised segments such as an FPA approach; it is the dynamic manoeuvres that need the attitude.
explanation.text: The bird shows where the aircraft is going, so it reacts only after the inertia of the aircraft has been overcome. In a dynamic manoeuvre such as a take-off or a go-around that delay makes it a poor reference, while the attitude responds at once to the sidestick. That is why, when TOGA is selected, the bird is removed automatically and the FD bars come back in SRS and GA TRK.

options.text: It lags behind in dynamic manoeuvres because of the aircraft inertia
It is removed whenever the AP is off
It is not computed when the gear is down
It shows only the track, not the flight path angle

questions.stem: Why should the bird (flight path vector) not be used as the flying reference during a go-around?

explanation.confuseWith: The star list is the normal display of secondary failures; ELEC EMER CONFIG is the exception.
explanation.text: No. After most primary failures the E/WD lists each affected system with a star. In ELEC EMER CONFIG the E/WD does not show that list: the secondary failures are inhibited. The crew uses the ELEC EMER CONFIG procedure, its STATUS page and the QRH summary to see what remains. The STATUS page still lists the systems that are inoperative.

options.text: Yes, each one with a star in front of its title
No, the secondary failures are then inhibited

questions.stem: ELEC EMER CONFIG. Does the E/WD list the secondary failures with stars, as after other primary failures?

explanation.confuseWith: In the descent the airspeed indicator reads too high, while the altimeter stays frozen.
explanation.text: It stays at the altitude where the blockage happened. The altimeter is a barometer: it measures the static pressure. With the port blocked, the trapped pressure no longer changes, so the altimeter freezes. The vertical speed indicator, also fed by static, shows zero, and the airspeed indicator, which compares pitot with the trapped static, reads too high in a descent and too low in a climb.

options.text: It stays at the altitude where the blockage happened
It shows the descent correctly
It drops to zero
It shows an altitude lower than the real one

questions.stem: The static port becomes blocked in cruise, the pitot stays clear. During a later descent, what does the altimeter show?

explanation.confuseWith: Yellow backs up the brakes, not the gear, and blue plays no part in gear operation.
explanation.text: Only the green hydraulic system powers the landing gear, moving every gear leg and every gear door. Two LGCIUs sequence the gear electrically, while green pressure does the work. Above 264 kt a safety valve shuts off this green supply. If green is lost, the crew lowers the gear with the hand crank, which isolates the gear hydraulics and lets gravity drop the gear.

options.text: Green
Blue
Yellow and Blue
Green and Blue.

questions.stem: Which hydraulic system(s) supply pressure to the landing gear system?

explanation.confuseWith: The memo reports a selector position set by the ground crew; it is not a steering failure detected by the system.
explanation.text: NW STRG DISC means that ground personnel have put the nose wheel steering selector into the towing position, which disconnects the steering. The selector is a lever on the towing electrical box at the nose landing gear. With it in the towing position the nose wheel can turn up to 95° either way, beyond the 75° the handwheel gives. The memo stays on the E/WD for as long as the selector remains in that position.

options.text: The nose wheel steering has been disconnected by ground personnel.
A failure in the nose wheel steering system has been detected.
There is a discrepancy between the two nose wheel steering handwheel positions
The nose wheel steering computer has finished its self test.

questions.stem: On the E/WD, you notice the NW STRG DISC memo. What does it mean?

explanation.confuseWith: Even after a training extension the reset is an in-flight action; on the ground after the flight it must not be done.
explanation.text: The free-fall system may be reset only after a gravity extension made for training, and only in flight with green hydraulic pressure available. The reset then lets the gear doors close. After a real gravity extension the procedure forbids a reset, because it could cause a further fluid loss through a leak, or a gear unlock if a selector valve is jammed in the UP position. A reset on the ground after the flight is not allowed either.

options.text: Yes, in flight, after any gravity extension.
Yes, in flight, but only after a gravity extension made for training.
Yes, but only on the ground, after a gravity extension made for training.
No, the free-fall system may never be reset.

questions.stem: May normal landing gear operation be restored after a gravity extension if green hydraulic pressure is available?

explanation.confuseWith: Seven brake applications is the accumulator's capacity for alternate braking; 12 hours is how long it holds the parking brake.
explanation.text: A parked aircraft keeps its brakes on accumulator pressure for 12 hours or more. When the parking brake is set, yellow pressure or accumulator pressure is applied in full to the main wheel brakes. The ACCU PRESS needle on the triple indicator shows the stored pressure, and the yellow electric pump can recharge the accumulator. With no yellow or accumulator pressure left, the normal brakes still respond to the pedals.

options.text: 6 hours.
12 hours.
18 hours.
24 hours.

questions.stem: The parking brake accumulator is designed to maintain the parking pressure for at least ______.

explanation.confuseWith: Below 750 ft a separate trigger uses thrust (both N1 below 75 %); flaps 3 with both radio altimeters failed needs no height.
explanation.text: Both situations trigger the GEAR NOT DOWN warning, so all of them apply. With the gear not downlocked, the warning comes with flaps 3 or FULL if neither radio altimeter works. It also comes below 750 ft radio height with flaps at 1, 2, 3 or FULL while the engines are not at take-off power, as in an approach. The red arrow next to the gear lever comes on with it.

options.text: Landing gear is not down locked and flaps 3 or full and both radio altimeters failed
Landing gear is not down locked, flaps at 3 and radio height lower than 750 ft
All of the above
None of the above.

questions.stem: During the approach you get master warning and ECAM “Gear Not Down”. The reason is:

explanation.confuseWith: VLE (280 kt) is the limit with the gear down; VLO extension (250 kt) is the limit for lowering it.
explanation.text: VLE, the highest speed with the landing gear extended, is 280 kt or M 0.67. It applies once the gear is down, for example when flying on with the gear stuck down. Moving the gear has lower limits: 250 kt (M 0.60) to extend it and 220 kt (M 0.54) to retract it. Abnormal procedures that leave the gear down, such as L/G GEAR NOT UPLOCKED, set a maximum speed of 280 kt / M 0.67.

questions.stem: The maximum speed with landing gear extended (VLE) is:

explanation.confuseWith: The doors and uplocks are released by the handcrank itself, not by the lever.
explanation.text: The lever is put DOWN so that the panel and the WHEEL page agree with the gear: the red UNLK lights go out and no L/G CTL message stays on the SD. The lever at DOWN also guards against a gear retraction on the ground if an unknown fault is present when the free-fall system is reset. The handcrank itself does the real work: three turns cut the hydraulic supply, unlock the doors and release the uplocks, and the gear falls.

options.text: To give the green system back to the gear for the landing
To clear the UNLK lights and prevent a retraction on the ground
To unlock the uplocks, which the handcrank only prepares
To open the gear doors, which the free fall does not do

questions.stem: After a gravity extension, why is the landing gear lever also set DOWN?

explanation.confuseWith: Switching off the pumps on the abnormal side would do the opposite and keep that wing heavy.
explanation.text: With one main gear missing, landing with the wing on that side lighter keeps it up longer, so the nacelle touches later. To get there, the QRH opens the crossfeed and switches off the pumps on the side whose gear is normally down, so both engines burn fuel from the other side, the side with the missing gear. If the fuel imbalance advisory then appears, it can be disregarded.

options.text: Open the crossfeed and switch off the pumps on the normal-gear side, so the wing without gear gets lighter
Keep both wings balanced, with the crossfeed closed
Open the crossfeed and switch off the pumps on the abnormal-gear side, so the wing with gear gets lighter
Switch off all centre tank pumps, so the CG moves aft

questions.stem: LANDING WITH ABNORMAL L/G: one main gear is not extended. What fuel action does the QRH suggest, and why?

explanation.confuseWith: The FCTM advises short applications, delayed to low speed if possible, not one long application at high speed.
explanation.text: By the time the parking brake is used, the LOSS OF BRAKING procedure has already removed the anti-skid, and the parking brake applies full pressure. So it is used in short, successive applications, delayed until the speed is low when possible. This reduces the risk of a tyre burst and of lateral control difficulty. An asymmetry may be felt at each application.

options.text: Preferably at low speed, in short applications
Only once the reversers have been stowed
At once at high speed, held on until the stop
At once, in one long application to save runway

questions.stem: LOSS OF BRAKING: alternate braking has not worked either, and the parking brake must be used. When should it be applied?

explanation.confuseWith: Tyre protection is the role of the fusible plugs, not of the take-off brake temperature limit.
explanation.text: After take-off the hot brakes are retracted into the wheel well. If a hydraulic leak sprayed fluid onto them there, a brake that is too hot could set it alight. The take-off brake temperature limit keeps the brakes cool enough to prevent that. With the brake fans running the indicated temperature reads lower than the real one, but the indicated value is still used, and the take-off is delayed above 150 °C.

options.text: So that the tyres do not deflate during the take-off roll
So leaking hydraulic fluid cannot ignite in the wheel well
So that the anti-skid can work during the take-off roll
So that the brake temperature sensors stay in range

questions.stem: Why is there a maximum brake temperature for take-off?

explanation.confuseWith: The blue pump pressurises the blue system only, which plays no part in braking.
explanation.text: The yellow electric pump does it: pressing the yellow ELEC PUMP pb pressurises the yellow system, and with it the brake accumulator. The accumulator backs up the alternate brakes and keeps the parking pressure. The blue system has no link with the brakes, and with both engines stopped the green system has no pressure of its own for the PTU to pass on. Setting the parking brake uses the pressure; it does not add any.

options.text: By switching the yellow ELEC PUMP pb ON
By setting the parking brake ON
By letting the PTU run from the green system
By pressing BLUE PUMP OVRD on the maintenance panel

questions.stem: On the stand with both engines stopped, the brake accumulator pressure is low. How can the crew recharge it?

explanation.confuseWith: The take-off mass includes the take-off fuel; the zero fuel mass stops before any usable fuel is added.
explanation.text: The zero fuel mass. The dry operating mass is the aircraft ready for the flight, with crew and their baggage, catering and equipment, but no usable fuel and no traffic load. Adding the passengers, baggage and cargo gives the zero fuel mass. Adding the take-off fuel then gives the take-off mass, and taking away the trip fuel gives the landing mass.

options.text: The landing mass
The basic empty mass
The zero fuel mass
The take-off mass

questions.stem: Which mass is the dry operating mass plus the traffic load?

explanation.confuseWith: 15° with TOGA is only for the phase below the thrust reduction altitude.
explanation.text: 10° with climb thrust. The memory items are used only when flight safety is at stake. AP, A/THR and FDs go off first, then the crew sets the pitch and thrust pair for the flight phase. Below the thrust reduction altitude it is 15° with TOGA; above it, 10° with CLB below FL 100 and 5° with CLB above FL 100. The crew also keeps the configuration, checks the speedbrakes retracted and the gear up, and levels off for troubleshooting at or above MSA or circuit altitude.

options.text: 15° / TOGA
10° / TOGA
10° / CLB
5° / CLB

questions.stem: UNRELIABLE SPEED INDICATION memory items, safe conduct of the flight affected. Above the thrust reduction altitude and below FL 100, which pitch and thrust?

explanation.confuseWith: The 2.5 s and 0.35 g response is for CLIMB NOW or INCREASE CLIMB, not for a first CLIMB RA.
explanation.text: For a corrective RA like CLIMB, the PF follows the green area within 5 s, smoothly and firmly, at about 0.25 g. A stronger or reversed order, such as CLIMB NOW or INCREASE CLIMB, needs a faster response: within 2.5 s at about 0.35 g. A preventive RA such as MONITOR V/S asks the crew not to change the flight path and to keep the vertical speed out of the red area. A TA alone never justifies a manoeuvre.

options.text: Within 5 s, smoothly and firmly at about 0.25 g
At once, with full sidestick deflection
Within 2.5 s, smoothly and firmly at about 0.35 g
Within 10 s, gently at about 0.1 g

questions.stem: TCAS corrective RA such as CLIMB. How quickly, and how firmly, should the PF follow the green area of the V/S scale?

explanation.confuseWith: GPWS SYS OFF would remove all basic GPWS modes; G/S MODE OFF removes only the glide slope alert.
explanation.text: Mode 5 warns of a descent below the glide slope. When the approach conditions call for a deliberate path below the beam, the procedure lets the crew set the G/S MODE pb-sw to OFF, which inhibits only that alert. When the path below the beam is not deliberate, the crew corrects the deviation while still high enough, and considers a go-around once below the stabilisation height of 1 000 ft (IMC) or 500 ft (VMC) above the airfield.

options.text: Set the TERR pb-sw to OFF
Set the G/S MODE pb-sw to OFF
Continue and ignore the repeated alert
Set the GPWS SYS pb-sw to OFF

questions.stem: The approach procedure deliberately requires flying below the glide slope, and the GPWS calls GLIDESLOPE. What may the crew do?

explanation.confuseWith: A go-around must be flown for TOO LOW GEAR or TOO LOW FLAPS; for SINK RATE low down it is only considered.
explanation.text: Below 1 000 ft AAL in IMC, or below 500 ft AAL in VMC, SINK RATE means the crew considers a go-around. Higher up, the crew adjusts pitch and thrust to silence the alert. TOO LOW GEAR and TOO LOW FLAPS, by contrast, always call for a go-around, and a PULL UP warning at night or in IMC calls for the full pull-up manoeuvre.

options.text: Fly the full pull-up manoeuvre
Adjust pitch and thrust to stop the alert
Perform a go-around at once
Consider a go-around

questions.stem: On approach in IMC at 800 ft AAL the TAWS calls SINK RATE. What does the memory item ask?

explanation.confuseWith: 15° is the pitch for STALL WARNING AT LIFTOFF and for unreliable speed below the thrust reduction altitude; the windshear figure is 17.5°.
explanation.text: When the FD bars are not displayed. Normally the PF follows the SRS orders, which already give the escape path. Without bars there is nothing to follow, so the memory items give a fixed initial pitch of 17.5° instead. If altitude is still being lost, the PF raises the pitch further; full backstick may be applied if necessary. The same rule applies after V1 at take-off and in the initial climb or at landing.

options.text: When the AP is engaged
When the FD bars are not displayed
Only during the take-off roll before V1
Whenever full backstick is applied

questions.stem: Windshear escape. In which case does the PF fly toward a fixed initial pitch attitude instead of following the SRS orders?

explanation.confuseWith: Starting the descent feels most urgent, yet the masks go on before it, and the signs come between the two.
explanation.text: Masks first, then the signs, then the descent. The procedure puts the protection of the crew before everything else, ahead of the passengers and of the descent itself. The signs come on for the passengers, and then the PF initiates the descent. With A/THR off, the thrust levers go to idle; ATC, the PA announcement and the squawk follow once the descent is established.

options.text: Crew oxygen masks, signs ON, descent initiated
Crew oxygen masks, descent initiated, signs ON
Descent initiated, crew oxygen masks, signs ON
Signs ON, crew oxygen masks, descent initiated

questions.stem: EMER DESCENT memory items. Which order of the first three actions is right?

explanation.confuseWith: A gust is shown with G right after the speed (24008G28KT), never with V, which marks a direction range.
explanation.text: The group gives the two extreme directions the wind blew from during the 10 minutes before the observation, written clockwise. It is added only when the total swing is 60° or more but under 180°, and the mean speed is at least 3 kt. Here the mean wind is 240° at 8 kt, swinging between 200° and 280°. For the runway crosswind check, both extremes matter, not only the mean.

options.text: The wind is forecast to veer from 200° to 280° within the next two hours
The wind is 200° at 8 kt, with gusts up to 28 kt
The wind direction varied between 200° and 280° during the last 10 minutes
The wind direction is variable, so the 240° figure is only an estimate

questions.stem: A METAR contains the wind groups 24008KT 200V280. What does 200V280 mean?

explanation.confuseWith: The dew point can never be higher than the temperature, so the second figure is always the lower or equal one.
explanation.text: The group gives the air temperature first and the dew point second, both in whole degrees Celsius, separated by a slash. The letter M in front means minus. Values from −9 °C to 9 °C carry a leading zero. A small gap between the two means moist air; with a temperature below zero, the crew watches for frost and icing on the ground.

options.text: Temperature −2 °C, dew point −5 °C
Minimum temperature −2 °C, maximum −5 °C
Temperature −5 °C, dew point −2 °C
Temperature 2 °C, dew point −5 °C

questions.stem: A METAR contains M02/M05. What does it mean?

explanation.confuseWith: Rime deposit is not required for FZFG; the temperature below 0 °C with droplets is enough.
explanation.text: FZ marks supercooled water: liquid droplets below 0 °C that freeze on contact. Fog made mainly of such droplets is freezing fog, FZFG, even if no rime is seen forming. For aircraft on the ground, freezing fog can build ice on the airframe, so it matters for de-icing and engine anti-ice decisions. Its onset or end is also a reason to mention it in a trend forecast.

options.text: When the visibility in fog is less than 200 m at a temperature below 0 °C
When the fog is made of ice crystals at a temperature below −10 °C
When the fog is mainly water droplets at a temperature below 0 °C, whether or not it deposits rime
Only when the fog is depositing rime ice on surfaces

questions.stem: When is fog reported as FZFG in a METAR?

explanation.confuseWith: Advection fog needs moist air moving over a colder surface, so it needs wind; it does not form in a calm.
explanation.text: Calm wind, clear sky and a temperature only 1 °C above the dew point are the classic set-up for radiation fog. On a clear night the ground loses heat by radiation and cools the air touching it to its dew point. Fog seldom forms when the spread is more than 2 °C, but here it is only 1 °C. Radiation fog forms over land, mostly at night, and usually lifts after sunrise or by noon.

options.text: Advection fog
Radiation fog
Clear air turbulence
Hail

questions.stem: At an inland aerodrome at 0300 local time, the METAR reads 00000KT CAVOK 06/05. What is the most likely hazard by dawn?

explanation.confuseWith: The type CB is attached only to the layer it belongs to; the broken layer at 4 000 ft carries no type.
explanation.text: Read it group by group. The wind is 310° at 18 kt with gusts of 32 kt, its direction swinging between 270° and 340°. Visibility is 10 km or more. The minus sign before the showers group means light rain showers. The first cloud group is a few cumulonimbus with base 2 500 ft above the aerodrome; the second is a broken layer at 4 000 ft with no type given. QNH is 1008 hPa and no significant change is expected for two hours.

options.text: Gusts reach 32 kt, there are light rain showers, and broken CB have their base at 4 000 ft
The mean wind is 32 kt, there are light rain showers, and a few CB have their base at 2 500 ft
Gusts reach 32 kt, there is heavy rain, and a few CB have their base at 2 500 ft
Gusts reach 32 kt, there are light rain showers, and a few CB have their base at 2 500 ft

questions.stem: METAR ZZZZ 121350Z 31018G32KT 270V340 9999 -SHRA FEW025CB BKN040 14/09 Q1008 NOSIG. Which statement is correct?

explanation.confuseWith: The gust must be at least 10 kt above the mean; being stronger is not enough.
explanation.text: 27014KT. A gust is added only when the highest gust is 10 kt or more above the mean speed. Here it is 8 kt above, so the gust is left out and only the 10-minute mean is reported. With a gust of 24 kt or more the group would read 27014G24KT. Peak gusts should represent a three-second average.

questions.stem: Over the last 10 minutes the mean wind was 270° at 14 kt, and the strongest gust reached 22 kt. How is the wind group coded?

explanation.confuseWith: The 1 000 m steps begin only at 5 000 m; at 3 450 m the step is 100 m.
explanation.text: 3400. Visibility is rounded down to fixed steps: 50 m up to 800 m, 100 m between 800 m and 5 000 m, and 1 000 m from 5 000 m up to 9 999 m, with 9999 meaning 10 km or more. 3 450 m lies in the 100 m band, so it goes down to 3 400 m. Rounding down never reports better visibility than observed.

questions.stem: The visibility meter shows 3 450 m. Which four digits does the METAR carry for the visibility?

explanation.confuseWith: A minute of longitude shrinks towards the poles; only a minute of latitude is always one nautical mile.
explanation.text: One minute of latitude, which is 1 852 m. Lines of latitude are equally spaced, so one minute of arc along a meridian is always the same distance; one degree is therefore 60 NM. Meridians come together towards the poles, so a minute of longitude equals one nautical mile only at the equator and less everywhere else.

options.text: One degree of latitude
One minute of longitude anywhere
One minute of latitude
One second of latitude

questions.stem: One nautical mile corresponds to:

explanation.confuseWith: The two types are managed (targets from the FMGS) and selected (targets from the FCU); manual flying is not one of them.
explanation.text: Managed and selected are the two kinds of guidance. In managed guidance the FMGS works out the targets itself and steers the aircraft along the planned route and the vertical and speed profiles. In selected guidance the crew sets the targets with the FCU knobs, for example a heading or a vertical speed, and the aircraft flies to them. Selected guidance always wins over managed guidance, so the crew can take over a target at any moment.

options.text: Slaved and managed.
Automatic and manual.
Managed and selected.
Managed and manual

questions.stem: What are the different types of flight guidance?

explanation.confuseWith: Targets that the crew sets on the FCU are selected guidance, not managed guidance.
explanation.text: In managed guidance the aircraft follows lateral, vertical and speed profiles worked out by the FMGS. The FMGS computes the aircraft position continuously and holds the planned route and the vertical and speed profiles, so it can compute the targets and steer along them. Selected guidance is the other case: the crew sets heading, speed or altitude on the FCU and the aircraft flies to those values. The ADIRS supply data to the FMGC; they do not compute profiles.

options.text: Guided by the pilot selecting the specific flight modes and parameter target values on the FCU.
Responding to pilot inputs of speed, altitude, and heading selected on the FCU.
Following lateral, vertical and speed profiles as determined by the IRS’S.
Following lateral, vertical and speed profiles as determined by the FMGS.

questions.stem: When the aircraft is in the Managed Guidance mode, it is:

explanation.confuseWith: With FMGC 1 failed, MCDU 1 stays usable because FMGC 2 serves it.
explanation.text: Either MCDU: with FMGC 1 failed the system runs in single mode, and an entry on either MCDU goes to the FMGC that still works. Both flight directors and both position monitor pages then use FMGC 2. On some FMS standards the MCDU on the failed side first shows the MCDU MENU page, and the crew connects it to the opposite FMGC with a prompt. The scratchpad then shows OPP FMGC IN PROCESS.

options.text: MCDU 1 on the Captain’s side.
MCDU 2 on the First Officer’s side.
Either MCDU 1 or MCDU 2.
No MCDU until FMGC 1 has been reset.

questions.stem: FMGC 1 is not working. To enter data into the FMGC, which MCDU would you use?

explanation.confuseWith: On the other display standard the DMCs have a single channel and only send data; the display units generate the images themselves.
explanation.text: True. On this display standard the three DMCs take in the signals from the sensors and the other computers and build the pictures for the PFDs, NDs, E/WD and SD themselves. Each DMC has two independent channels, one for EFIS and one for ECAM, so it can drive one PFD, one ND and one ECAM display at the same time. The SDACs feed them the system data for the system pages and engine parameters.

options.text: True
False

questions.stem: On aircraft whose DMCs each have an EFIS and an ECAM channel, the three Display Management Computers (DMCS) acquire and process all input from airplane sensors and computers to generate the display images.

explanation.confuseWith: The scale itself stops at 30 kt; slower speeds are not shown at all, not even as a number.
explanation.text: 30 kt: the PFD airspeed scale does not show values below 30 kt. The scale is white on a grey background and moves behind a fixed yellow reference line. The same 30 kt is the bottom of the ISIS speed scale, and it is also the lowest value accepted for an ISIS speed bug.

options.text: 100 kts.
80 kts
50 kts.
30 kts

questions.stem: The airspeed indication on the PFD starts at:

explanation.confuseWith: The value becomes the target only when the knob is pulled; nothing engages by itself.
explanation.text: The selection is lost and the dashes come back. In managed speed the SPD/MACH window is dashed. Turning the knob shows a value (the current target plus the turn), but this is only a preselection: the crew must pull the knob to engage selected speed on it. If the knob is not pulled, the value stays for 10 s on the SPD/MACH window (45 s on HDG/TRK and V/S) before the dashes return.

options.text: The selection can be made at any time.
The selection is lost and dashes are re-displayed.
The selection is lost and the display goes blank.
The new value engages automatically after 10 seconds.

questions.stem: If the SPD/MACH knob on the FCU is not pulled within a predetermined time to engage selected speed:

explanation.confuseWith: With both RAs lost, G/S cannot be used, so lateral guidance comes only through the LOC pb, not APPR.
explanation.text: LOC only. With both radio altimeters failed, the STATUS page shows that the LOC modes remain, armed and captured with the LOC pb, but G/S capture and track are not available. CAT 2 is lost as well. The approach is flown with LOC guidance only, and the vertical path is the crew's task. The landing is made in CONF 3 at VREF + 10 kt, and the flight controls go to direct law when the gear is down.

options.text: G/S only, with the lateral path flown in TRK
None: the approach is flown on raw data only
LOC only, through the LOC pb; no G/S modes
LOC and G/S through the APPR pb, CAT 1 only

questions.stem: NAV RA 1 AND 2 FAULT. Which ILS guidance modes are still available for the approach?

explanation.confuseWith: Switching to ADR 3 restores the F/O air data; the baro check is a separate consequence of the ADR 2 loss.
explanation.text: With ADR 2 failed, a single FCU channel drives both baro reference channels. The ECAM therefore asks the crew to check the baro reference displays: the FCU and both PFDs should show the same setting. The other actions are to switch the F/O air data to ADR 3 and to set ADR 2 OFF. The STATUS page then shows CAT 3 SINGLE ONLY.

options.text: The transponder now reports QNH altitude instead of STD
ADR 3 does not receive any baro setting
The standby altimeter takes its setting from ADR 2
A single FCU channel now drives both baro references

questions.stem: NAV ADR 2 FAULT. After selecting ADR 3 on the F/O side, why does the ECAM ask for a BARO REF check?

explanation.confuseWith: ALL keeps a symmetric ±2 700 ft window; the 9 900 ft extension comes only with ABV or BLW.
explanation.text: ALL shows proximate and other intruders all the time within 2 700 ft above and below. ABV extends the window upward to 9 900 ft above while keeping 2 700 ft below, which suits a climb; BLW does the opposite for a descent. THRT shows intruders only when a TA or RA is present. Only the eight most threatening intruders are displayed in any case.

options.text: BLW: up to 9 900 ft above and 2 700 ft below
THRT: up to 2 700 ft above and below
ALL: up to 9 900 ft above and below
ABV: up to 9 900 ft above and 2 700 ft below

questions.stem: In climb, the crew wants to see traffic well above the aircraft on the ND. Which TRAFFIC selector position gives the widest view upward?

questions.context: On aircraft with the EXPED pb.

explanation.confuseWith: 340 kt or M 0.80 is the descent target; in climb EXPED flies green dot.
explanation.text: EXP CLB flies green dot, and EXP DES flies 340 kt or M 0.80. In both cases the AP/FD holds the speed with the pitch, the A/THR sets climb thrust or idle, and all altitude and speed constraints and the speed limit are disregarded. Either mode engages only after at least 5 s airborne, with managed speed available.

options.text: 340 kt or M 0.80 in climb; green dot in descent
Green dot in climb; 340 kt or M 0.80 in descent
340 kt or M 0.80 in both climb and descent
Green dot in both climb and descent

questions.stem: Which speed targets does EXPED use in climb and in descent?

explanation.confuseWith: 0 °C is the freezing point; the limitation already counts from 10 °C.
explanation.text: 10 °C. In flight the limitation looks at the TAT; on the ground and after take-off it looks at the OAT. In both cases the value is 10 °C or colder, together with some visible moisture: cloud, fog that cuts visibility to 1 600 m or less, or any precipitation or ice crystals. On the ground, slush, snow or standing water on the surfaces at that temperature also counts, as the engines may ingest it or it may freeze on them.

questions.stem: By the limitations, icing conditions exist in flight when visible moisture is present and the TAT is at or below which value?

explanation.confuseWith: 230 kt is the limit for CONF 1 (slats only); with the flaps still out in 1+F it is 215 kt.
explanation.text: 215 kt is the limit for CONF 1+F, because the flaps are still out as well as the slats. With the lever at 1 the aircraft can be in two configurations: 1+F, with slats and flaps, limited to 215 kt, and 1, slats only, limited to 230 kt. If the crew does not select flaps 0, the flaps run in by themselves at 210 kt, just before the limit is reached, and the slats stay out.

options.text: 200 kt
185 kt
215 kt
230 kt

questions.stem: After take-off the FLAPS lever is at 1 and the display shows 1+F. What is the maximum speed?

explanation.confuseWith: 8.6 PSI is the safety valve setting, which stays below the 9.0 PSI limit.
explanation.text: 9.0 PSI is the structural limit for the cabin pushing outwards. The safety valve is set lower, at 8.6 PSI, so that it opens before the limit is reached. On the other side, the maximum negative differential, with outside pressure higher than inside, is 1.0 PSI. Both the limit and the valve setting carry a tolerance of about 0.1 PSI.

options.text: 8.0 PSI
9.0 PSI
8.6 PSI
1.0 PSI

questions.stem: What is the maximum positive cabin differential pressure?

explanation.confuseWith: The maximum flexible temperature is the upper limit of TFLEX, not a lower one.
explanation.text: TFLEX may be neither lower than the flat rated temperature TREF nor lower than the actual OAT; both are floors, and the crew must respect the higher of the two. The maximum flexible temperature is the opposite end of the band, the highest TFLEX allowed. A FLEX take-off is also allowed only if the aircraft meets every performance requirement with the thrust of that temperature, and never on a contaminated runway.

options.text: The actual OAT only
The flat rated temperature (TREF) and the actual OAT
The flat rated temperature (TREF) only
TMAXFLEX and the actual OAT

questions.stem: Below which temperatures may the FLEX temperature (TFLEX) not be set?

explanation.confuseWith: The FMGS is certified for navigation, but its fuel and time predictions remain advisory.
explanation.text: No. The FMS fuel, time and performance predictions are for advisory purposes only. In cruise the crew also checks FOB plus fuel used against the departure figure. The FMGS approval also assumes a validated navigation database, and obstacle clearance stays a crew responsibility, whatever mode is flown.

options.text: Yes, they may replace the crew's own fuel checks
No, they are for advisory purposes only

questions.stem: Are the FMS fuel and time predictions certified as primary information?

explanation.confuseWith: Pilot reports can make the assessment worse, not better than the runway condition allows.
explanation.text: No. The crew first assesses the runway condition from the type and depth of the contaminant. Friction measurements or pilot reports of braking action may be used in addition, but the landing distance must not be based on a better braking action than the one tied to that runway condition. With more than 3 mm of slush the limit is MEDIUM TO POOR, whatever a report says.

options.text: Yes, a pilot report overrides the runway condition
No, it may not assume better than the runway condition gives

questions.stem: A pilot report gives braking action GOOD on a runway covered with slush deeper than 3 mm. May the landing distance be based on GOOD?

explanation.confuseWith: It is a recommended ceiling from certification, not a certified limitation like VMO or the flap speeds.
explanation.text: False. 38 kt, gust included, is the strongest crosswind met during the certification flights, so it is a demonstrated value, not an AFM limitation. Airbus recommends that operators do not plan to go beyond it. On wet or contaminated runways the recommended crosswind is lower and falls with the runway condition code, down to 15 kt on ice.

options.text: True
False

questions.stem: The maximum demonstrated crosswind is an AFM limitation that may never be exceeded. True or false?

explanation.confuseWith: 70 kt limits maximum reverse, not idle reverse.
explanation.text: True. The low-speed limit applies to maximum reverse only: it should not be used once the aircraft has slowed below 70 kt. Idle reverse is a different case, and it may stay selected until the aircraft has come to a full stop. Two other uses are never allowed: selecting reverse in flight, and using reverse thrust to move the aircraft backwards on the ground.

options.text: True
False

questions.stem: Idle reverse thrust may be kept until the aircraft has stopped. True or false?

explanation.confuseWith: The cabin pressure page shows pressurisation, not the oxygen figure.
explanation.text: The crew oxygen cylinder pressure appears as a figure in PSI on the DOOR/OXY system page of the lower ECAM display. The oxygen shares that page with the doors, so it is easy to look for the figure on the wrong page. The figure stays green while the pressure is normal and turns amber when it is low. On the ground, a low figure is the cue to compare it with the minimum crew oxygen pressure in the limitations.

options.text: The PRESS page.
The DOORS page.
The COND page.
The STATUS page.

questions.stem: On which ECAM page could the flight crew check the exact pressure of the oxygen cylinder?

explanation.confuseWith: MASK MAN ON also works through the electrical latches, so it does not help when the power has failed.
explanation.text: Each mask container is held shut by an electrical latch that opens automatically at the release cabin altitude, or when the crew presses MASK MAN ON. If an electrical failure prevents this, crew members can open the container doors with a manual release tool. After the masks have been restowed, the system can be reset for rearming, and the PASSENGER SYS ON light stays on until a maintenance reset.

options.text: By resetting the system with TMR RESET
With the manual release tool
By pressing MASK MAN ON again
They cannot be opened without power

questions.stem: An electrical failure stops the passenger oxygen mask doors from opening. How can they be opened?

explanation.confuseWith: The factors are added, not multiplied, and the larger one alone is not enough.
explanation.text: The trip fuel penalty is the fuel still to be burnt (fuel on board minus the estimated fuel on board at destination) multiplied by the sum of the applicable factors. These factors are conservative guideline values. The FMS predictions must then be recomputed with this penalty. A factor applies only if the conditions in its table row, such as a surface shown extended, are really met.

options.text: Trip fuel on the FMS × (FPF1 + FPF2), with no recomputation
(FOB − EFOB at destination) × the larger factor only
(FOB − EFOB at destination) × (FPF1 + FPF2)
(FOB − EFOB at destination) × FPF1 × FPF2

questions.stem: After two failures, two fuel penalty factors (FPF) apply. How is the trip fuel penalty computed?

explanation.confuseWith: The lowest direct operating cost defines ECON Mach, not LRC.
explanation.text: LRC is the Mach number at which the specific range, the distance flown per unit of fuel, is 99 % of the best possible. It is a speed defined by range, not by cost. It differs from ECON Mach, which minimises direct operating costs for a given cost index. With one engine out, the FMS EO mode computes an engine-out LRC instead.

options.text: The Mach giving 99 % of the maximum specific range
The Mach giving the lowest direct operating cost
The Mach giving the maximum specific range
The Mach giving 95 % of the maximum specific range

questions.stem: How is the long range cruise speed (LRC) defined?

explanation.confuseWith: 45 kt is the point where the credit stops, not a limit on taking off.
explanation.text: No. Unlike the tailwind, which is limited to a certified value, the headwind has no certified maximum. A headwind above 45 kt simply gives no further performance credit, and only half of any entered headwind is counted in the computation in any case. The crosswind part of the wind is limited separately, according to the runway condition, and the take-off technique changes with a tailwind or a strong crosswind.

options.text: Yes, 45 kt is the certified headwind limit
No, but above 45 kt it brings no extra performance credit

questions.stem: Is there a maximum certified headwind for take-off?

explanation.confuseWith: Fan air is used only to cool the bleed air in the pre-cooler, not as the bleed source.
explanation.text: Bleed air normally comes from the IP stage of the engine's high-pressure compressor, because that costs the least fuel. At low engine speed, when IP air is too weak or too cool, the HP valve opens and the system takes air from the HP stage, holding it at 36 ± 4 PSI. A check valve then stops HP air from flowing back into the IP stage.

options.text: High pressure stage.
Intermediate stage.
Low pressure stage.
Fan stage.

questions.stem: Bleed air normally comes from the _______ of the engine.

explanation.confuseWith: The wings have a double loop, so a wing leak normally needs both loops to agree.
explanation.text: The pylon and APU leak detection uses a single loop. Sensing loops run beside the hot air ducts of the fuselage, the pylons and the wings and react to any overheating. In the wings the sensing elements form a double loop, and a wing leak signal needs both loops, or one loop when the other is inoperative. Both bleed monitoring computers carry the same leak logic.

options.text: The pylons and APU.
The wings and pylons.
The wings and fuselage.
The wings and APU.

questions.stem: The overheat detection system uses a single loop for:

explanation.confuseWith: Low-pressure ground air is a separate connection that feeds the mixer unit directly, not the pneumatic system.
explanation.text: High-pressure air has three sources: the two engine bleed systems, the APU load compressor and the high-pressure ground connection. A crossbleed duct links the engine bleed systems and takes in air from the APU and from the ground source when appropriate. A valve on that duct can join or separate the left and right sides. Two bleed monitoring computers control and monitor the system.

questions.stem: High pressure air has ______ sources.

explanation.confuseWith: Only an engine start keeps the valve open despite a leak signal, not a flight or ground phase.
explanation.text: With the X BLEED selector at AUTO, the crossbleed valve opens whenever APU bleed air is used, so that the APU can supply both sides. If an air leak is detected in a wing, a pylon or the APU, the valve closes to isolate the leak, except during an engine start, when the air is needed for the starter. The valve has two electric motors, one for the automatic mode and one for the manual OPEN and SHUT positions.

options.text: It closes if the system detects an air leak (except during engine start).
It closes if the system detects an air leak (except in flight).
It closes if the system detects an air leak (except on the ground).
It stays open if the system detects an air leak (except during engine start).

questions.stem: In automatic mode, the crossbleed valve opens when the system is using APU bleed air.

explanation.confuseWith: At AUTO the APU selection opens the crossbleed and closes both engine valves; at SHUT engine 2 keeps the right side.
explanation.text: Engine 2 keeps supplying it, because with the APU bleed ON and the crossbleed valve SHUT, the engine 2 bleed valve stays open. The APU air then serves the left side, where the engine 1 bleed valve has closed as usual for an APU bleed selection. The crossbleed valve is the only link between the left and right sides, so with it shut the two sides stay separate.

options.text: By the APU, through the crossbleed duct
It is not supplied: engine 2 bleed valve closes
By engine 1, through the pack 1 duct
By engine 2, whose bleed valve stays open

questions.stem: APU BLEED is ON with both engines running, but the X BLEED selector is at SHUT. How is the right side supplied?

explanation.confuseWith: The stall speed is only the speed at which the critical angle is reached in given conditions; it changes with weight and load factor.
explanation.text: The critical angle of attack. Beyond it the airflow separates from the upper surface and lift falls away. The angle is fixed for a given wing and configuration, but the speed at which it is reached rises with weight, load factor and bank. So a wing can stall at any speed and in any attitude. The A320 protections therefore watch the angle of attack, not the speed alone.

options.text: The critical angle of attack
A maximum pitch attitude
A minimum indicated airspeed
A maximum load factor

questions.stem: A wing stalls when which value is exceeded?

explanation.confuseWith: Induced drag is high at low speed and falls as speed rises; parasite drag is the one that rises with speed.
explanation.text: Induced drag decreases and parasite drag increases. Induced drag comes from making lift. At low speed the wing needs a high angle of attack, so induced drag is large, and it falls as the speed rises. Parasite drag comes from pushing the airframe through the air and grows with the square of the speed. The total is lowest where the two are equal, at the minimum drag speed.

options.text: Both decrease
Induced drag increases, parasite drag decreases
Both increase
Induced drag decreases, parasite drag increases

questions.stem: As the speed increases in level flight, what happens to induced drag and parasite drag?

explanation.confuseWith: Below 4 A marks the end of the charging cycle, not the 10 s check.
explanation.text: Setting the BAT pb-sw OFF then AUTO starts a charging cycle of the batteries. About 10 s later the current of each battery should be below 60 A and falling. If a battery is not yet below 60 A, the crew waits for the end of the charging cycle and checks again. The cycle itself ends when the charge current falls below 4 A.

options.text: Battery charge current below 60 A and decreasing
Battery charge current below 4 A
Battery charge current above 60 A and rising
No current: the battery contactors are open

questions.stem: Cockpit preparation: BAT 1 and BAT 2 are set OFF, then AUTO. What is checked on the ELEC SD page 10 s later?

explanation.confuseWith: APU bleed may never feed wing anti-ice; it is not used for take-off if wing anti-ice is needed.
explanation.text: Packs take bleed air from the engines, so with the packs off, or fed by the APU, each engine does less work for the same thrust. On a FLEX take-off this lowers the EGT and so the maintenance cost; on a TOGA take-off it gives more performance. FLEX itself saves the most in its first few degrees. APU bleed is not used for take-off when wing anti-ice will be needed, because APU air may never supply it.

options.text: Lower take-off EGT, and so lower engine maintenance costs
It protects the engines against a stall at take-off thrust
The cabin is pre-pressurised without the packs
APU bleed can then supply wing anti-ice

questions.stem: FLEX take-off. What is the benefit of selecting the packs OFF, or supplying them with APU bleed?

explanation.confuseWith: Sequencing is about the missed approach, the ND picture and the predictions, not about arming the approach modes.
explanation.text: In NAV mode the flight plan sequences by itself, but in HDG it does so only when the aircraft passes close to the route. If the old waypoints stay, the missed approach may not be ready for a go-around, and distances and the vertical deviation are wrong. The TO waypoint on the ND is a good check. The fix is DIR TO RADIAL IN, or clearing the FROM waypoint until the next likely waypoint is the TO waypoint.

options.text: Because LOC cannot arm with an unsequenced flight plan
So the ILS frequency is tuned automatically
So that the HDG mode is not lost when APPR is pressed
So the missed approach is available for a go-around and the predictions are correct

questions.stem: Radar vectors in HDG mode, and the waypoints do not sequence. Why must the crew sequence the flight plan before the approach?

explanation.confuseWith: MORE DRAG belongs to a descent already flown above the profile in DES; in level flight past the T/D the message is T/D REACHED or DECELERATE.
explanation.text: Past the computed top of descent, every mile flown level puts the aircraft further above the ideal path. The PFD and MCDU show T/D REACHED or DECELERATE, which suggests slowing towards green dot speed, if ATC agrees, so that less energy has to be lost later. When the descent clearance comes, the crew engages DES with managed speed.

options.text: DECELERATE; extend flaps 1 to slow down in level flight
MORE DRAG; extend the speed brakes to stay on the profile
T/D REACHED; start an OP DES at once, without waiting for ATC
T/D REACHED or DECELERATE; reduce towards green dot with ATC agreement

questions.stem: ATC delays the descent, and the aircraft passes the T/D in cruise. What does the FMS show, and what should the crew do?

explanation.confuseWith: The danger is not a firm touchdown but the high pitch used to avoid one, which reduces the tail clearance.
explanation.text: Most landing tail strikes come from departures from the normal technique. Holding the aircraft off for a smooth touchdown keeps the pitch rising, and as the nose goes up the pilot looks further ahead and misjudges the attitude, so the pitch can pass the critical angle. A speed well below VAPP before the flare, a too high flare, a high sink rate near the ground and raising the pitch after a bounce have the same effect.

options.text: A prolonged hold-off to get a very smooth touchdown
Keeping the thrust at idle after a light bounce
Keeping VAPP until the flare height
Thrust levers to idle at the RETARD callout

questions.stem: Which of these landing techniques increases the risk of a tail strike?

explanation.confuseWith: 25° of bank is the circling approach figure for the final turn, not the visual circuit one.
explanation.text: The final turn onto the runway centreline starts with about 20° of bank. The descent begins gently, at about 400 ft/min, and increases to about 700 ft/min once the aircraft is on the correct descent path. Landing configuration and VAPP must be reached no lower than 500 ft above the airfield, or the crew goes around.

options.text: 25° of bank; 700 ft/min at first, then 1 000 ft/min on the descent path
30° of bank; 400 ft/min throughout
15° of bank; 1 000 ft/min at first, then 700 ft/min on the descent path
20° of bank; 400 ft/min at first, then 700 ft/min on the descent path

questions.stem: Visual circuit, final turn. Which bank angle and rates of descent does the FCTM give?

explanation.confuseWith: The PTU transfers pressure, not fluid, so it cannot change the quantities between systems.
explanation.text: A slight fall in hydraulic quantity in cruise is expected. The fluid contracts when it is cold-soaked at altitude, and the green system reads lower than on the ground once the gear has been retracted. The PTU only transfers power between green and yellow, never fluid.

options.text: It is normal: fluid contracts in the cold, and green is lower after gear retraction
The reservoir pressurisation has failed
A slow leak, so the crew applies the HYD RSVR LO LVL procedure
The PTU has moved fluid from the green to the yellow system

questions.stem: In cruise the HYD SD page shows the fluid quantities slightly lower than on the ground. What does this mean?

explanation.confuseWith: An absence of ECAM alerts does not prove the structure is intact after a tailstrike.
explanation.text: After a tailstrike the aircraft must be checked for damage, so the crew avoids any altitude that needs a pressurised cabin and returns to the departure airport for a damage assessment. The SOP guards against a tailstrike by rotating at about 3°/s toward 15° and following SRS, and by avoiding a fast rotation near the ground in a go-around.

options.text: Continue to destination below FL 250
Avoid altitudes needing a pressurised cabin and return for an inspection
Continue normally if no ECAM alert appears
Climb to cruise level and depressurise the cabin

questions.stem: A tailstrike occurs at take-off. What does the SOP caution say?

explanation.confuseWith: A transducer fault is one cause of a wrong oil reading in flight, but in a cold start the viscosity is the expected reason.
explanation.text: In cold weather the engine oil is thick, and during the start the oil pressure indication may show amber XX for that reason alone. The crew can expect this. After the first engine start, probe and window heat goes back to AUTO, and the heating then goes on working automatically.

options.text: The oil pressure transducer has failed; stop the start
The cold oil is very viscous; this can be expected
The FADEC has lost the oil pressure channel
The oil quantity is too low; stop the start

questions.stem: Engine start after a cold night. The oil pressure shows amber XX during the start sequence. What is the likely cause?

explanation.confuseWith: A stronger headwind raises the optimum Mach; it does not lower it.
explanation.text: The ECON Mach depends on the cost index, the level, the temperature deviation, the weight and the headwind. So the optimum Mach rises as the headwind grows. The FCTM gives a rule of thumb: about M 0.01 more for each 50 kt of extra headwind. A weaker headwind lowers it again. The A/THR flies the new Mach automatically in managed speed.

options.text: It increases by about M 0.01
It decreases by about M 0.01
It does not change; only the OPT FL changes
It increases by about M 0.05

questions.stem: In cruise in managed Mach, the headwind increases by 50 kt. How does the optimum Mach change?

explanation.confuseWith: A fixed percentage added to the distance is not the method; a second computation with the worse condition is.
explanation.text: If the weather is expected to change, or with significant precipitation, the runway condition at arrival may be worse than the one reported now. A second in-flight landing distance computed with the worst possible runway condition shows in advance whether the landing would still be possible. If conditions have changed since dispatch, both pilots compute the landing distance independently, and the EFB must take the MEL and CDL items into account.

options.text: Compute a second in-flight landing distance with the worst possible runway condition
Wait until the latest ATIS before computing anything
Use the dispatch landing distance, which already covers it
Add 15 % to the current in-flight landing distance

questions.stem: Descent preparation: heavy showers are forecast at the destination and the weather may change. What does the SOP suggest for the landing distance?

explanation.confuseWith: 50 ft is the correction at 500 ft for a -10 °C airport in the FCTM table, far smaller than this case.
explanation.text: In cold air the true altitude is lower than the barometric altitude shown, so published minimum altitudes are corrected upward. For a sea-level airport the correction is about 4 × ΔISA × height / 1 000: 4 × 25 × 2 000 / 1 000 = 200 ft. The correction applies to the FAF, the step-down altitudes, the minima and the altitude and distance checks. The flown FPA is also shallower than the one computed.

options.text: About 100 ft
About 50 ft
About 200 ft
About 500 ft

questions.stem: Approach to a sea-level airport, 25 °C colder than ISA. The FAF is published at 2 000 ft above the airport. Using the FCTM rule of thumb, about how much should be added to it?

explanation.confuseWith: The thrust stays frozen, not reduced, and the extra bleed demand shows up as a higher EGT.
explanation.text: Taking the pack air from the APU keeps the engines at their no-bleed performance while the cabin is air-conditioned. If the APU shuts down during the take-off, the engine thrust is frozen until the crew reduces it manually. The packs then take engine bleed air, and the EGT rises as the engines hold the same N1 or EPR.

options.text: Thrust stays frozen; packs take engine bleed and EGT rises
The FADEC reduces N1 to protect the EGT
The packs close and stay off until the crew selects them ON
